paper.title: Sulforaphane inhibits N-nitrosodimethylamine induced hepatocellular carcinoma stem cell properties via ZNF652/Sonic hedgehog axis.
paper.journal: Frontiers in cell and developmental biology
paper.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: N-Nitrosodimethylamine (NDMA) is a potent carcinogen implicated in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) pathogenesis and cancer stem cell (CSC) emergence. Zinc finger protein ZNF652 exhibits tumor-suppressive properties, while Sonic Hedgehog signaling promotes CSC characteristics. Sulforaphane (SFN), a natural compound, shows anticancer potential, but its regulatory role in NDMA-induced liver CSCs remains unclear. This study aimed to investigate the ZNF652/Sonic Hedgehog axis in NDMA-induced liver CSCs and elucidate SFN's inhibitory effects through this pathway.

METHODS: An in vitro NDMA-induced HCC cell model and in vivo xenograft experiments were combined with molecular analyses to explore mechanisms. Bioinformatics analyses evaluated ZNF652's prognostic significance and Sonic Hedgehog pathway correlation. In vitro experiments induced LO2 cell malignant transformation via chronic NDMA exposure, performed sphere formation assays, and validated ZNF652/GLI1 interactions through overexpression, downregulation, and dual-luciferase assays. In vivo subcutaneous xenograft models treated with SFN (12.5/25 mg/kg) demonstrated dose-dependent tumor suppression, reduced CD133/GLI1 expression, and restored ZNF652 levels.

RESULTS: Chronic NDMA exposure (1 μg/mL) transformed LO2 hepatocytes into malignant TLO2 cells with CSC traits, including elevated HCC, CSC and EMT markers. ZNF652 expression decreased in metastatic HCC tissues and NDMA-induced CSCs. Overexpressing ZNF652 reduced sphere formation, suppressed CSC markers (CD133, SOX2, OCT4, EPCAM), and inhibited Sonic Hedgehog pathway activity by directly targeting GLI1 via promoter binding. SFN treatment diminished CSC self-renewal, downregulated GLI1 expression, and reversed ZNF652 knockdown-induced CSC properties in vitro. In nude mouse xenografts, SFN dose-dependently reduced tumor volume/weight, lowered CD133/GLI1 levels, and restored ZNF652 expression compared to NDMA-exposed group.

CONCLUSION: SFN inhibits NDMA-induced liver cancer stemness via the ZNF652/Sonic Hedgehog axis, offering a novel therapeutic strategy for hepatocellular carcinoma.
paper.full_text:
Introduction
Liver cancer is a widespread cancer globally (Bray et al., 2024), and is classified into primary liver cancer (PLC) and secondary liver cancer (SLC). Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) accounts for 90% of PLC cases and is a major cause of mortality among patients (McGlynn et al., 2021; Li et al., 2021a). The etiology of HCC is multifactorial, often arising from chronic hepatitis virus infection, hormonal disparities, and dietary and environmental factors (Li et al., 2021a; Rumgay et al., 2022). Consumption of aflatoxin-contaminated foods, preserved and smoked foods (Li et al., 2021b), as well as high levels of nitrate in water and soil (Chen et al., 2023; Cai et al., 2023), contribute to excessive intake of carcinogenic nitrosamines, triggering HCC development (Yin et al., 2024). N-nitrosodimethylamine (NDMA) is one such nitrosamine found abundantly in preserved and smoked foods, exhibiting potent carcinogenic, teratogenic, and mutagenic properties (Lu R. Q. et al., 2021; Schrenk et al., 2023). The liver is the primary target organ for NDMA, and prolonged low-dose exposure predisposes individuals to the onset of HCC (Zheng et al., 2021; Mansouri et al., 2022). Studies have demonstrated that prolonged exposure to NDMA can cause liver cancer in animals (Laothong et al., 2013; Souliotis et al., 2002). Creating a model of NDMA-induced liver cancer cells helps replicate primary liver cancer progression, aiding in understanding its mechanism and treatment.

Despite the development of early liver cancer diagnosis and intervention methods, advanced cases still carry a poor prognosis with high rates of metastasis and recurrence. Cancer stem cells (CSCs) are characterized by self-renewal, multi-differentiation, and strong tumorigenicity (Skvortsova, 2018), and contribute to metastasis, recurrence and resistance to treatment, worsening the prognosis for HCC patients (Oikawa, 2016). Therefore, uncovering the molecular pathways of liver CSCs is crucial for comprehending liver cancer development.

Zinc finger (ZNF) proteins are most common transcription factors in the human (Jen and Wang, 2016). ZNF652, a member of ZNF family, is typically expressed at low levels in cancer tissues, including HCC (Kumar et al., 2006). Several studies demonstrate that increased ZNF652 expression significantly inhibits tumor development, inhibits tumor immune evasion, and suppresses tumorigenesis and progression (Liu et al., 2023). These results underscore the potential of ZNF652 in cancer intervention. However, while some studies have linked high ZNF652 expression with poor tumor prognosis, the role of ZNF652 in liver CSCs remains unclear.

The Sonic Hedgehog pathway is a classical cancer-associated pathway (Ruiz i Altaba et al., 2002). Dysregulation of Sonic Hedgehog pathway occurs frequently and promotes tumor development. Aberrant Sonic Hedgehog signaling may contribute to the development of HCC. GLI1, a crucial component of this pathway, can directly activate Hedgehog signaling by translocating into the nucleus (Takebe et al., 2015). Recent studies have shown that GLI1 is abnormally high in tumor cells (Jiang, 2022). Elevated GLI1 expression enhances Sonic Hedgehog signaling in liver CSCs (Zhang et al., 2014). Therefore, GLI1 is a potential target in CSCs intervention.

Sulforaphane (SFN), an isothiocyanate found in cruciferous vegetables, exhibits anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and anticancer properties. Numerous studies have reported inhibitory effects of SFN on various tumors, including liver cancer (Rausch et al., 2010; Moon et al., 2010). However, the precise regulatory mechanisms of SFN on CSCs remain incompletely understood. Therefore, this study aimed to elucidate the mechanisms by which SFN executes inhibitory effect on liver CSCs.

Cell culture
Human liver cell line LO2 and liver cancer line Huh-7 were purchased from Chinese Academy of Sciences. TLO2 cells were transferred from LO2 cells which were treated with 1 μg/mL NDMA (Sigma, Cat No. 62-75-9) for 30 times of passages (3 months). LO2 and TLO2 were cultured in RPMI 1640 (Gibco, United States of America), Huh-7 was cultured in DMEM (Gibco, United States of America), supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS) (Gibco, United States of America) and penicillin/streptomycin mixture (Beyotime, China). All cells were cultured in a 37 °C incubator containing 5% CO2.

Diagram illustrating LO2 cell exposure to solvent control or two concentrations of NDMA (zero point one and one microgram per milliliter) across thirty passages, producing CLO2, TLO2-I, and TLO2-II cell lines, with subsequent functional assays for proliferation, self-renewal, migration, invasion, epithelial-mesenchymal transition, and stem cell-like capacity.

Colony formation assay
Cell spheroids were separated into single cells by trypsin and then 500 cells were seeded into dishes. After culture in RPMI 1640 medium for 10 days, the colonies were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde for 30 min. Crystal violet was used to stain colonies for 10 min.

Anchorage-independent growth assay
Soft agarose dishes were precoated with 0.7% agarose (Beyotime, China) in RPMI-1640 medium. CLO2, TLO2, and Huh-7 cells were resuspended into single cells and 5,000 cells were seeded into agarose. After culture for 2 weeks, colonies with diameters >50 μm were counted.

Transwell assays
About 5 × 104 CLO2, TLO2, and Huh-7 cells were resuspended in serum-free medium and seeded in the upper chamber of 24-well migration chambers (Corning, United States of America, 3422). For cell invasion, the upper chambers were precoated with Matrigel (Corning, United States of America, 356234). The lower chambers were filled with 800 μL medium supplemented with 10% FBS. The chambers were incubated for 24 h. Cotton swabs were used to wipe away cells remained in the upper chambers. Crystal violet (Beyotime, China) was used to stain the cells under the surface of the chambers. Images of migrated and invaded cells were taken under a microscope.

Sphere-forming assay
TLO2 and Huh7 cells were suspended in DMEM-F12 medium (Gibco, United States of America) supplemented with 5 μg/mL insulin, 20 ng/mL basic fibroblast growth factor, 20 ng/mL epidermal growth factor (Rocky Hill, United States of America), and 2% B27 (Gibco, United States of America). The number of spheres bigger than 50 μm was calculated under the microscope. SFN was purchased from Sigma (Cat No. 4478-93-7, purity≥ 98%).

TLO2 and Huh-7 cells were suspended in DMEM/F-12 medium (Gibco, United States of America) supplemented with 5 μg/mL insulin, 20 ng/mL basic fibroblast growth factor, 20 ng/mL epidermal growth factor, and 2% B27 (Gibco, United States of America).1 × 107 Cells were seeded in 6 cm dishes and cultured for 7 days. Cells were gently triturated once daily, and half of the culture medium was replaced with fresh sphere-forming medium every 2 days. At the end of culture, spheres with a diameter >50 μm were counted under a microscope. This experiment represented primary sphere formation. SFN was purchased from Sigma (Cat. No. 4478-93-7, purity ≥98%).

CCK-8 assay
Cells were seeded into 96-well plates at a density of 5,000 cells per well and cultured for 48 h. Subsequently, CCK-8 reagent was added to each well and incubated for 2 h at 37 °C. The absorbance was measured at 450 nm using a microplate reader.

Western blot analysis
Cells were lysed in lysis buffer (Beyotime Biotechnology) and the concentration of proteins was determined by BCA kit (Beyotime, China). Total proteins were separated by SDS-PAGE and transferred to nitrocellulose membrane (Millipore, United States of America). The membrane was probed with primary antibodies overnight, then with secondary antibodies for 40 min, and detected with enhanced chemiluminescence (MD Bio, China). GAPDH served as the loading control. ZNF652 antibody was purchased from Origene (United States of America), GLI1, SHH, SMO, GLI2, CD133, OCT4, EPCAM, SOX2 and GAPDH were purchased from Proteintech (China).

Flow cytometry
Cells were stained with APC-CD133 antibody (Miltenyi Biotech, Germany) or APC-IgG for 30 min at 4 °C, and then separated into single cells for detection by FACS AriaIII system (Becton-Dickinson, United States of America). The results were analyzed by FlowJo software.

Real-time PCR
Total RNA was isolated with Trizol (Yifeixue Biotech, China) and purified with RNA pure reagent. cDNA was synthesized with 5×All-In-One RT MasterMix (Applied Biosystems, United States of America). PCR was performed with EvaGreen 2×qPCR MasterMix (Applied Biosystems, United States of America) and LC96 real-time PCR system (Roche, Switzerland) with the following primers:

GAPDH (ID: 2597)

forward, 5′-CAA​GGT​CAC​CAT​GAC​AAC​TTT​G-3′;

Reverse, 5′-GTC​CAC​CAC​CCT​GTT​GCT​GTA​G-3′;

ZNF652 (ID: 22,834)

Forward, 5′- GCT​GGT​TGA​AAA​CTG​TGC​TGT-3′;

Reverse, 5′- GAA​GAT​GGC​ACT​TGA​CCA​CGA-3′.

Transient transfection
The GLI1 and ZNF652 overexpression plasmid and vector were purchased from Genechem (China). The GLI1 and ZNF652 siRNA were purchased from Santa Cruz. Cells were cultured to 60%-70% density and maintained in RPMI 1640 without FBS before transfection. Plasmids or siRNAs were transfected with lipofectamine 2000 reagent (Invitrogen, United States of America) according to the manufacturer’s instruction. Cells were cultured in RPMI 1640 supplemented with 10% FBS after transfection.

Dual-luciferase reporter assay
The luciferase reporter plasmids containing wild type and mutant GLI1 promoter in psiCHECK 2 vector were purchased from Genomeditech (China). Cells were seeded in 24-well plates, and co-transfected with the plasmids using lipofectamine 2000 reagent. Luciferase activity was detected using dual-luciferase reporter kit (Promega, United States of America) after 48 h.

Immunofluorescent staining
Cell spheres were seeded in 24-well plate for immunofluorescent staining, fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde, sealed in 5% BSA, and permeabilized with 0.5% Triton X-100. Then spheres were incubated with primary antibodies at 4 °C overnight. After washing with PBS for 3 times, spheres were incubated with fluorescent secondary antibody at 25 °C in the dark. The nuclei were stained with 4′6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (Beyotime, China). Images of spheres were taken under confocal microscopy (Zeiss, Germany).

Extreme limiting dilution analysis (ELDA)
Cells were seeded into 96-well plates at different density and maintained in DMEM/F-12 medium. Five days after treatment with different concentrations of SFN, the number of cell spheres per well (bigger than 50 μm) was counted under the microscope, and data were calculated on the ELDA website https://bioinf.wehi.edu.au/software/elda/.

Animal experiments
A cohort of 20 female BALB/c nude mice, aged 4-week, were provided by Jiangsu GemPharmatech Animal Laboratory Center (China) and housed at Experimental Animal Center at Nanjing Medical University. All animal experiments were performed in accordance with the National Institutes of Health Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals, and the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of Nanjing Medical University (IACUC-2211062) approved the protocol.

After acclimatization, mice were randomly divided into 4 experimental groups (control group, NDMA-induced group, SFN low dose group, SFN high dose group, n = 5/group), Huh-7 cells after different treatments (4 × 106 per mouse) were injected subcutaneously into mice. Except for control group, Huh-7 cells in three experimental groups were pretreated with NDMA (1 μg/mL) for 2 weeks prior to inoculation to mimic chronic NDMA exposure. Seven days after injection, mice received oral gavage treatments twice weekly: control and NDMA-induced groups were administered with 100 μL 0.9% sodium chloride solution, while low dose and high dose SFN groups were administered with 12.5 mg/kg and 25 mg/kg SFN, respectively. Mice were monitored regularly for body weight, health status, and tumor dimensions. After 28days of treatment, xenograft tumors were surgically excised, weighed and preserved appropriately.

Immunohistochemistry (IHC)
Following dehydration, paraffin embedding, and sectioning, tumor tissues were incubated with primary antibodies at 4 °C for 16 h, followed by incubation with secondary antibody at 37 °C for 60 min. Chromogenic visualization was performed using 3,3′-diaminobenzidine (DAB, Biosharp, China), and observed under microscope.

Statistical analysis
All data were presented as mean ± standard deviation (SD) and analyzed by using SPSS 11.0 software. The difference between two groups was calculated by Student’s t-test, and among multiple groups was calculated by one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) along with Dunnett or Bonferroni post hoc test. The significance was set at p < 0.05.

Establishment of liver cancer cells with chronic NDMA exposure
To simulate primary liver cancer, we established NDMA-induced HCC cellmodel. LO2 cells were continuously treated with 0.1 μg/mL and 1 μg/mL NDMA for 30 passages. Cells treated with 0.1 μg/mL NDMA were labeled as TLO2-I, and those treated with 1 μg/mL NDMA were labeled as TLO2-II. Control cells without NDMA exposure were labeled as CLO2. The Huh-7 cell line was employed as a phenotypic positive control for comparative validation. Compared to CLO2 cells, TLO2-II cells exhibited noticeable morphological changes, appearing irregular in shape, spindle-shaped, or elongated (Figure 1A), and showed significantly higher proliferation rates (Figure 1B). In addition, the migration and invasion abilities of TLO2-II cells increased compared to CLO2 cells, even surpassing those of Huh-7 cells (Figures 1C,D). We examined the levels of HCC markers AFP, GGT1, GSTP1 and epithelial-mesenchymal transition markers (Vimentin, N-cadherin, ZO-1, E-cadherin) in NDMA treated cells and found that the levels of HCC markers and mesenchymal markers increased in TLO2-II cells, while levels of epithelial markers markedly decreased (Figure 1E). These results suggest that with chronic exposure to NDMA, TLO2-II cells successfully transformed from normal liver cells into HCC-like cells, while TLO2-I cells underwent a less malignant transformation.

Next, we established a sphere-forming culture model and employed serum-free medium (SFM) treatment to enrich liver CSCs population. The, enrichment of stem cells with SFM led to significantly increased size and quantity of cell spheres in TLO2-II and Huh-7 groups compared to CLO2 and TLO2-I groups (Figures 1F,G). Soft agar assay indicated that NDMA could promote anchorage-independent growth of TLO2-II cells (Figure 1H). Colony formation assay demonstrated markedly enhanced colony-forming ability of TLO2-II cells, comparable to the mature liver cancer cell line Huh-7, while TLO2-I cells showed similar capability to CLO2 cells (Figure 1I). Moreover, the expression levels of stem cell-related markers CD133 and OCT4 in the four cell types after sphere formation were higher in TLO2-II than in CLO2 and TLO2-I, comparable to Huh-7 levels (Figure 1J). These results suggest enhanced stem cell characteristics in liver cancer cell line induced by NDMA. In our subsequent experiments, we will utilize TLO2-II cells as experimental model and designate them as TLO2.

Enrichment of liver CSCs after sphere-forming
To validate that TLO2 cells exhibit stem cell characteristics, we subjected them to SFM suspension enrichment. As shown in Figure 2A, TLO2 and Huh-7 cells aggregated into a cellular sphere under SFM conditions, showing notable differences in morphology compared to cells cultured in serum-supplemented medium (SSM). Furthermore, the mRNA and protein levels of liver CSC markers (CD133 [PROM1], SOX2, OCT4 [POU5F1], and EPCAM) were higher in SFM-treated group than in SSM-treated group (Figures 2B,D). Flow cytometry analysis revealed approximately 25% increase in CD133+ cells (p < 0.05) in SFM group after sphere-forming (Figure 2C). These findings indicate the acquisition of CSC characteristics in TLO2 sphere-forming cells under SFM condition.

ZNF652 inhibits CSC properties of liver CSCs
To reveal the role of ZNF652 in HCC, we conducted survival analysis using the KM-PLOTTER database. Higher expression of ZNF652 was related to higher survival rate and longer survival (Figure 3A), suggesting a potential role of ZNF652 in inhibiting HCC. We further analyzed the expression levels of ZNF652 in HCC tissues, normal tissues, and metastatic lesions using the TNMPLOT database. The expression of ZNF652 was lower in liver tumor issues to normal tissues (Figure 3B), suggesting that ZNF652 may inhibit HCC.

Subsequently, we assessed protein expression of ZNF652 in liver CSCs and observed downregulation in SFM group (Figure 3C). To elucidate the role of ZNF652 in liver CSCs, we overexpressed ZNF652 in TLO2 and Huh-7 cells (Figures 3D,E). We observed smaller sphere size and significantly reduced sphere frequency in ZNF652 overexpression group compared to vector group (Figure 3H). Western blot analysis revealed lower expression of CSC markers CD133, SOX2, OCT4, and EPCAM (Figure 3I). Conversely, the knockdown of ZNF652 (Figures 3F,G) resulted in a larger sphere size and higher sphere frequency compared to control group (Figure 3J), accompanied by upregulation of CSC markers (Figure 3K). These findings suggest that ZNF652 is downregulated in liver CSCs and could inhibit CSC-like properties of liver CSCs.

Sonic hedgehog signaling promotes CSC properties in HCC
Analysis of TIMER2.0 database showed elevated expression levels of key components of sonic Hedgehog signaling including SHH, SMO, GLI1, and GLI2 in liver cancer tissue compared to normal liver tissue (Figure 4A, Supplementary Figures S1A–C). Next, we assessed mRNA and protein expression of key markers of sonic hedgehog pathway in liver CSCs. Compared to SSM group, SHH, SMO, GLI1, and GLI2 levels were notably higher in SFM group, indicating upregulation of Sonic Hedgehog pathway in liver CSCs (Figures 4B,C).

Moreover, we regulated GLI1 expression level to modulate Sonic Hedgehog pathway. After GLI1 overexpression (Figures 4D,F), we observed the increase in both the size and the frequency of spheres (Figure 4H). Additionally, GLI1 overexpression led to higher protein levels of liver CSC markers compared to the vector group (Figure 4J). Conversely, when GLI1 expression was reduced (Figures 4E,G), the size and frequency of spheres decreased (Figure 4I), accompanied by notable decline in CSC marker expression (Figure 4K). These findings illustrate regulatory role of GLI1 and Sonic Hedgehog pathway in liver CSC properties.

ZNF652 directly targets GLI1 in liver CSCs
To investigate the relationship between ZNF652 and Sonic Hedgehog pathway, we utilized the TNMplot database. Our analysis revealed a negative correlation between the expression of ZNF652 and key components of Sonic Hedgehog pathway, including SHH, SMO, and GLI1 (Figure 5A, Supplementary Figures S2A–B). These findings suggest a potential inhibitory effect of ZNF652 on Sonic Hedgehog pathway. Therefore, we examined the expression of Sonic Hedgehog pathway components following the modulation of ZNF652 expression. Overexpression of ZNF652 led to significant decrease in both mRNA and protein levels of Sonic Hedgehog signaling pathway components (Figures 5B,D). Conversely, knockdown of ZNF652 led to notable upregulation of SHH, SMO, GLI1, and GLI2 mRNA and protein levels (Figures 5C,D). These findings suggest that ZNF652 may inhibit Sonic Hedgehog pathway.

To further investigate the role of ZNF652 in regulating Sonic Hedgehog pathway, we focused on GLI1. Exploring JASPAR databases revealed potential binding sites between ZNF652 and GLI1 (Figure 5E). To confirm the transcriptional activity of this binding site, we constructed wild type and mutant luciferase reporters (Figure 5F). Dual-luciferase assay results showed that ZNF652 overexpression inhibited GLI1 transcriptional activity (Figure 5G), indicating that ZNF652 can directly target GLI1 and suppress GLI1-associated Sonic Hedgehog signaling pathway.

Next, we investigated whether ZNF652 regulation of GLI1 influences CSCs properties. Immunofluorescence analysis revealed that GLI1 overexpression significantly increased CD133 fluorescence intensity. However, co-transfection of ZNF652 after GLI1 upregulation resulted in decreased CD133 expression (Figure 5H), suggesting that ZNF652 can counteract GLI1-induced CSC properties. Similarly, GLI1 downregulation reversed the increase in CSC properties caused by ZNF652 downregulation (Figure 5I). These data demonstrate that ZNF652 directly targets GLI1 to inhibit CSC properties of liver CSCs.

SFN inhibits CSC-like properties in liver cancer
SFN, a well-known isothiocyanate compound, exhibits anti-cancer effects in various tumors. Therefore, we treated TLO2 cells with different concentrations of SFN (0, 1, 3, 5 μM). As shown in Figures 6C,D, SFN treatment significantly reduced the size and frequency of spheres. Colony formation assay demonstrated that SFN inhibited colony formation in TLO2 spheroids (Figure 6A). Moreover, ELDA revealed that SFN suppressed the self-renewal capacity of liver CSCs (Figure 6B).

Western blot analysis showed downregulation of CD133, SOX2, OCT4, and EPCAM expression following SFN treatment (Figure 6F). Additionally, the fluorescence intensity of CD133 decreased notably after SFN treatment, in correlation to SFN concentration (Figure 6E). These findings demonstrate that SFN inhibits CSC properties in liver cancer.

SFN mediates ZNF652/GLI1 axis and inhibits CSC properties in liver cancer
Next, we investigated the effect of SFN on Sonic Hedgehog pathway. SFN downregulated protein levels of markers in Sonic Hedgehog pathway (Figures 7A,B). In addition, the increase in self-renewal capacity of liver CSCs due to GLI1 overexpression was reversed after SFN treatment, accompanied by the reversal in the expression levels of CSC markers (Figures 7C–F). These findings suggest that SFN inhibits CSC properties of liver cancer by suppressing GLI1 expression.

Considering that ZNF652 regulates GLI1, the effect of SFN on CSC properties may be controlled via ZNF652/GLI1 axis. The expression level of ZNF652 increased after SFN treatment (Figures 7G,H). Following SFN treatment, the size and frequency of spheres affected by ZNF652 downregulation increased (Figures 7K,L). Additionally, the expression levels of ZNF652 and GLI1 were reversed by SFN treatment (Figures 7I,J). Furthermore, compared to ZNF652 downregulation group, CD133 expression decreased after SFN treatment (Figures 7K,L). These results demonstrate that SFN can inhibit CSC properties by mediating ZNF652/GLI1 axis in liver CSCs.

SFN inhibits NDMA-induced liver CSC properties in vivo
Previous studies demonstrate that SFN suppresses NDMA-induced liver cancer stem-like properties in vitro. To validate in vivo effects, HCC xenograft model was established. Mice injected with NDMA-exposed Huh7 had significantly increased tumor volume compared to control group (Figure 8B,E). SFN-treated groups exhibited dose-dependent decreases in tumor volume/weight compared to NDMA group, confirming SFN-mediated inhibition of NDMA-induced hepatocarcinogenesis. IHC analysis (Figure 8F) demonstrated elevated CD133 (stemness marker) expression in NDMA-treated tumors compared to control group, while SFN treatment reduced CD133 levels compared to NDMA group. GLI1, a key molecule of Sonic Hedgehog pathway, showed increased expression in NDMA-treated tumors, which was suppressed by SFN. Conversely, NDMA exposure downregulated ZNF652 expression, while SFN dose-dependently reversed this suppression. Overall, these results demonstrate that SFN can inhibit NDMA-induced CSC properties via ZNF652/GLI1 axis in liver cancer.

Discussion
As a major risk factor for HCC, NDMA plays an important role in hepatocarcinogenesis. In this study, prolonged low-dose NDMA exposure induced HCC-like changes in LO2 cells and enhanced stem-like characteristics, as reflected by sphere formation and CSC marker expression. We further found that ZNF652 was involved in the regulation of these properties and was functionally associated with GLI1/Sonic Hedgehog signaling. SFN also affected this regulatory axis, suggesting a possible mechanism underlying its inhibitory effects on NDMA-associated CSC properties.

Evidence suggests that the acquisition of stemness following nitrosamine exposure may occur during the early stages of cancer development. Chronic exposure to NDMA has been associated with HCC development (Wang et al., 2022), and the related nitrosamine compound DEN has been reported to enhance stemness characteristics in experimental liver cancer models (Liu et al., 2021; Sawong et al., 2022). However, it remains unclear whether NDMA can promote stemness characteristics in HCC. In this study we showed that prolonged exposure to NDMA increased colony formation, induced EMT-like changes in CSCs, and upregulated the expression of liver CSC markers (CD133, EPCAM, SOX2, and OCT4). These results suggest that NDMA promotes the transformation and CSC-like properties in human hepatocytes.

ZNF652 has been reported to be expressed at relatively low levels in several tumors and to be associated with tumor invasion and progression (Kumar et al., 2006; Holm et al., 2008). High ZNF652 expression has also been associated with favorable prognosis in lung adenocarcinoma (Xu et al., 2020). In HCC, however, the expression pattern of ZNF652 appears to be more complex. Our database analysis showed higher ZNF652 expression in HCC tissues than in normal tissues, whereas lower expression was observed in metastatic lesions, and higher ZNF652 expression was associated with better survival. These findings suggest that the role of ZNF652 may vary according to tumor stage or biological context. Consistent with a possible suppressive role in stemness, ZNF652 expression was reduced after sphere enrichment, and modulation of ZNF652 affected sphere formation and CSC marker expression. Although circ-ZNF652 has been reported to promote HCC progression (Li et al., 2020), circ-ZNF652 and the ZNF652 protein represent different molecular entities and may have distinct biological functions.

Sonic Hedgehog pathway plays an important role in tumor (Jeng et al., 2020), and promotes CSC properties (Kundu et al., 2022), including HCC (Wu et al., 2024; Gu Y. et al., 2021). Previous studies have shown that activation of this pathway contributes to liver tumor initiation and fibrosis-associated hepatocarcinogenesis (Wu et al., 2024; Chung et al., 2016). Our data further suggest a link between ZNF652 and this pathway. A predicted ZNF652-responsive region was identified in the GLI1 promoter, and reporter assays supported transcriptional regulation of GLI1 by ZNF652. Together with the functional rescue experiments, these findings support GLI1 as an important downstream mediator of ZNF652-associated regulation of CSC properties.

Targeting tumor stem cells holds considerable promise as a therapeutic strategy against tumors. Several studies have reported the potential of SFN in inhibiting various types of cancer (Liu et al., 2024; Lu Z. et al., 2021), also been reported to reduce carcinogen-associated inflammation and tumor development (Zhang et al., 1994; Bonnesen et al., 2001). Moreover, SFN has been shown to inhibit the characteristics of CSCs and hinder tumor recurrence and metastasis (Xie et al., 2019; Gu H. F. et al., 2021). Ongoing clinical trials on SFN have demonstrated its capacity to inhibit cancer development and extend patient survival (Mangla et al., 2021; Livingstone et al., 2022). In the present study, SFN reduced sphere formation and CSC marker expression and was accompanied by increased ZNF652 expression and reduced GLI1-associated Hedgehog signaling. These findings suggest that modulation of the ZNF652/GLI1 axis may contribute to the inhibitory effect of SFN on NDMA-associated CSC-like properties.

Several limitations should be considered when interpreting our findings. The in vivo experiments relied on xenografts established from NDMA-pretreated Huh-7 cells rather than systemic NDMA exposure in mice, and thus may not fully reproduce the natural course of NDMA-associated hepatocarcinogenesis or the complex hepatic microenvironment. In addition, the human database analyses are correlative and indicate a potentially context-dependent pattern of ZNF652 expression in HCC. As these observations were not independently validated in clinical specimens, further studies using well-defined patient cohorts and human tissue samples will be important to confirm their translational relevance.

In conclusion, this study reveals important role of ZNF652/Sonic Hedgehog axis in regulating NDMA induced liver CSC properties and inhibitory effects of SFN on these cells. Our findings provide support for SFN intervention in NDMA-associated HCC.

paper.title: Orchestrating cancer stem cell plasticity: deubiquitinases as key regulators of EMT and metabolic rewiring.
paper.abstract: Cancer stem cells (CSCs) drive tumor relapse, metastasis, and multidrug resistance, primarily attributed to their profound phenotypic plasticity. This plasticity largely depends on the dynamic interplay between the epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) program and metabolic reprogramming. However, the molecular mechanisms coordinating these processes remain incompletely elucidated. Emerging evidence suggests that deubiquitinating enzymes (DUBs) may participate in regulating this complex crosstalk. This review systematically elaborates on the functional roles of DUBs in maintaining CSC characteristics within malignancies, exploring how they regulate CSC fate by modulating developmental signaling cascades (Wnt/β-catenin, Hedgehog (Hh), Notch, and TGF-β). By preventing the proteasomal degradation of key transcription factors, DUBs simultaneously drive EMT and coordinate metabolic reprogramming to meet the energetic demands of migrating CSCs. Furthermore, we emphasize the bidirectional feedback loops between EMT-TFs and DUBs, which cooperatively amplify stemness. Finally, selective targeting of the DUB-EMT-metabolism axis may represent a potential strategy for dismantling CSC plasticity and improving responses to anticancer therapies.
paper.full_text:
Introduction
Cancer stem cells (CSCs) are increasingly recognized as the primary drivers of tumor heterogeneity, as well as key forces behind recurrence, distant metastasis, and therapeutic resistance (1). Emerging evidence suggests that CSCs establish specialized niches within the tumor microenvironment, maintaining their stem-like properties through dynamic interactions with fibroblasts, immune cells, and the extracellular matrix. This unique microenvironment further enhances their resistance to therapy. Although conventional chemotherapy and radiotherapy can eliminate a large number of proliferating tumor cells, they often fail to completely eradicate CSCs, leading to recurrence, metastasis, and cancer-related mortality (2). A distinctive feature of CSCs is their remarkable plasticity. Beyond self-renewal and tumor initiation, CSCs can reversibly shift between different phenotypic states in response to microenvironmental cues and therapeutic stress (3). Among the processes underlying this plasticity, epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) has received particular attention. Through EMT, epithelial tumor cells lose apical-basal polarity and intercellular adhesion, while upregulating mesenchymal markers such as Vimentin (VIM) and Snail. To support the energetic demands of metastasis, tumor cells undergo metabolic reprogramming and enhance their migratory capacity by activating pathways such as Wnt/β-catenin and TGF-β (4).

Clinical evidence indicates that tumors containing a high proportion of CSCs are significantly associated with poor prognosis. In breast cancer, CSC enrichment increases the 3-year recurrence risk by 2.8-fold and significantly shortens progression-free survival (PFS) (5). Similarly, a colorectal cancer cohort study linked elevated CD133⁺ CSC levels to a 42% decrease in 5-year survival rates. On this basis, putative CSC-associated markers such as ALDH1 and CD44 have been investigated for their potential prognostic value. These observations also provide a rationale for further evaluating the CSC regulatory network as a potential therapeutic target, although its clinical utility remains to be established.

Molecularly, EMT is characterized by the loss of epithelial adhesion molecules, particularly E-cadherin (CDH1), and the concomitant upregulation of mesenchymal markers like VIM and N-cadherin (CDH2). This process, which confers migratory and invasive properties on cells, is primarily driven by EMT transcription factors (EMT-TFs), including the Snail (Snail1/2), Twist (Twist1/2), and ZEB (ZEB1/2) families (6). Emerging evidence underscores a bidirectional regulatory network between EMT and metabolic reprogramming in CSCs, which is crucial for maintaining tumor stemness. EMT-TFs can directly drive metabolic shifts by modulating enzyme expression; for instance, Twist1 enhances glycolysis in lung cancer via the Wnt/β-catenin pathway (7). Furthermore, Twist1 is a key regulator of aerobic glycolysis in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC); its depletion severely impairs glucose consumption, lactate secretion, and extracellular acidification (8). Conversely, the metabolic intermediates generated by these reprogramming events can retroactively regulate EMT. For instance, in hypoxic PDAC cells, hypoxia-inducible factor-1α (HIF-1α) upregulates glycogen phosphorylase L (PYGL) in the quasi-mesenchymal subpopulation. PYGL mobilizes glycogen reserves to fuel glycolysis, thereby promoting EMT progression (9). Similarly, aldehyde dehydrogenase 1A3 (ALDH1A3) sustains CSC stemness and coordinates EMT by balancing oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) and glycolysis while maintaining reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels (10).

The ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS) is essential for intracellular protein homeostasis. As a key component of the UPS, deubiquitinating enzymes (DUBs) reverse ubiquitination modifications by hydrolyzing ubiquitin chains on target proteins, thereby modulating their stability, subcellular localization, and activity (11). Consequently, DUB dysregulation causes aberrant accumulation of downstream substrates, including EMT-TFs and metabolic enzymes, ultimately driving tumor initiation and progression. To date, approximately 100 DUBs have been identified and classified into six structural families: ubiquitin-specific proteases (USPs), ubiquitin C-terminal hydrolases (UCHs), ovarian tumor proteases (OTUs), Machado-Joseph disease proteases (MJDs), JAB1/MPN/Mov34 metallo-proteases (JAMMs), and the MINDY family (12). Due to the large number of USP family members and their strong association with cancer, it remains the most extensively studied family. Notably, USP2, USP10, and USP37 are frequently overexpressed in CSCs of various malignancies, where they maintain stemness by stabilizing specific EMT-TFs or metabolic enzymes (13–15).

Although growing evidence indicates that DUBs independently modulate EMT and tumor metabolism, a comprehensive framework integrating their roles in the bidirectional crosstalk between these processes in CSCs is still lacking. Specifically, how DUBs may coordinate this interaction across different tumor types—and whether such regulation follows pan-cancer or context-dependent patterns—remains unclear. To examine this issue, this review summarizes the functional characteristics of DUBs and their molecular roles in EMT-metabolism crosstalk. Furthermore, we propose a multilayered regulatory model in which DUBs may act as regulatory nodes connecting EMT activation, metabolic rewiring, epigenetic regulation, and ferroptosis evasion, thereby potentially contributing to multidrug resistance and tumor progression (Figure 1). Rather than conceptualizing DUBs as static enzymes interacting with single substrates, we emphasize that their biological effects are dictated by dynamic substrate selection across distinct cellular states. DUB substrate specificity is determined by multiple factors, including subcellular localization, cell-type-specific expression patterns, adaptor and scaffold proteins, ubiquitin-chain linkage preferences, post-translational modifications, and the signaling landscape of the tumor microenvironment. These variables explain both why the same DUB can target different substrates in distinct microenvironments and why individual DUBs can exert either oncogenic or tumor-suppressive functions in a context-dependent manner. For instance, this explains how USP7 (also known as HAUSP) differentially regulates β-catenin, DNA methyltransferase 1 (DNMT1), glioma-associated oncogene homolog (Gli), or transformation/transcription domain-associated protein (TRRAP) depending on the specific molecular context. Consequently, this review transcends a systematic catalog of DUB-substrate pairs to provide a framework for understanding how DUB-dependent regulatory networks modulate CSC plasticity, metastatic progression, and therapeutic sensitivity.

Expression and functions of DUBs in CSCs
Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most aggressive astrocytic neoplasm of the central nervous system (CNS). Within GBM, glioblastoma stem cells (GSCs) represent a functionally distinct subpopulation with tumor-initiating capacity. These cells are the major contributors of tumor recurrence, therapeutic refractoriness, and metastasis, making them important therapeutic targets (16).

Ubiquitin-Specific Protease 1 (USP1) is aberrantly overexpressed in primary human GBM tissues and patient-derived GSCs (16). Mechanistically, USP1 maintains the GSC phenotype by stabilizing two key substrates: Inhibitor of Differentiation 1 (ID1) and Checkpoint Kinase 1 (CHEK1). ID1 promotes stemness by upregulating the pluripotency factor SOX2 and downregulating the kinase inhibitor p21Cip1/Waf1 (17). Meanwhile, CHEK1 is crucial for the DNA damage response (DDR) cascade; its activated form (p-CHEK1) is maintained at high intracellular levels by USP1, thereby driving GSC radioresistance (18). USP1 overexpression induces a significant shift toward a stem-like state, characterized by elevated expression of SOX2 and Olig2, alongside suppression of the astrocytic differentiation marker GFAP and the cell cycle regulator p21. Notably, ID1 and p-CHEK1 are significantly enriched in GSCs compared to the bulk tumor population (16). Collectively, USP1 maintains GSCs and drives radiotherapy resistance by stabilizing regulators of both stemness and DDR signaling pathways, highlighting its translational potential as a novel therapeutic target for GBM.

Breast cancer stem cells (BCSCs) drive tumor initiation, metastatic dissemination, therapeutic resistance, and relapse. Emerging evidence indicates that DUBs maintain BCSCs by modulating epigenetic regulators and stemness-associated signaling networks. For instance, lysine-specific demethylase 1 (LSD1) is an epigenetic regulator controlling H3K4 methylation dynamics, and it is enriched at genomic loci governing pluripotency and differentiation blockade. USP28 directly stabilizes LSD1 via deubiquitination, thereby enhancing the stem-like features of breast cancer cells (19). Accordingly, depletion of USP28 upregulates differentiation-associated genes, including p21Cip1/Waf1, HNF4, HoxA10, and FoxA2. Thus, the USP28-LSD1 axis maintains the undifferentiated state and self-renewal capacity of BCSCs by antagonizing the differentiation program (19).

USP44 is closely associated with an aggressive BCSC phenotype. Specifically, the USP44-positive BCSC subpopulation promotes vasculogenic mimicry, a phenomenon tightly linked to tumor invasiveness and poor prognosis (20). Clinically, enrichment of USP44+ tumor stem-like cells is associated with poor patient outcomes, indicating that USP44 serves as both a functional driver of BCSC aggressiveness and a prognostic biomarker (21).

Beyond GBM and breast cancer, DUBs also play key roles in regulating CSC phenotypes in various malignancies. In renal cell carcinoma, for example, USP21 is significantly upregulated in stem-like cells, driving self-renewal through two complementary mechanisms. First, it binds the interleukin-8 (IL-8) promoter to directly upregulate its transcription (22). Second, it stabilizes Gli1 via a protein kinase A (PKA)-dependent phosphorylation cascade, thereby activating the Hedgehog (Hh) signaling pathway. Similarly, in colorectal cancer, USP54 is significantly enriched in CSCs and is associated with shortened overall survival, although the specific mechanism by which it mediates CSC maintenance remains to be elucidated (23). Collectively, these findings establish the concept that DUBs orchestrate stem-like phenotypes by regulating transcriptional programs, DDR signaling, developmental pathways, and epigenetic states, further confirming their potential as viable therapeutic targets.

Functional intersection of EMT and CSCs
Substantial evidence indicates a profound interconnection between EMT and CSC characteristics: cells undergoing EMT frequently acquire stem-like properties, while CSCs reciprocally exhibit EMT markers along with enhanced migratory and invasive capabilities (24). In mammary epithelial cells (MECs), induction of EMT generates a transcriptome resembling that of mesenchymal stem cells, conferring multilineage differentiation and augmented wound-healing potential. Consistent with this, Mani et al. demonstrated that inducing EMT in MECs expands the CD44+/CD24− stem-like population and endows it with tumor-initiating capacity (25). Crucially, these phenotypic transitions are accompanied by extensive metabolic rewiring—highlighting the tight integration of EMT, stemness, and metabolism. Similarly, in prostate cancer, cancer-associated fibroblasts not only induce EMT in tumor cells but also enhance stemness markers, sphere-forming ability, and self-renewal capacity (26, 27). In summary, these findings underscore the biological interdependence and coordinated regulation between EMT and CSC programs.

Key DUBs in the regulation of EMT
DUBs may participate in the EMT-CSC crosstalk by modulating the stability of several signaling intermediates, transcription factors, and chromatin regulators. For example, the tumor-suppressive CYLD attenuates NF-κB signaling. In esophageal cancer stem-like cells, the STAT3/miR-181b axis downregulates CYLD, thereby enhancing proliferation and anti-apoptotic capacity (28). Simultaneously, loss of CYLD potentiates Notch signaling (29), which upregulates Snail and N-cadherin to promote the EMT process. Similarly, USP7, as a multifaceted DUB, plays a central role in both CSC maintenance and EMT. It maintains stemness by deubiquitinating TRRAP, thereby promoting the expression of stemness-related genes such as MYC (30). In epithelial ovarian cancer, USP7 acts synergistically with the E3 ligase MARCH7 to suppress E-cadherin and upregulate β-actin, driving canonical EMT events (31). Furthermore, USP7 interacts with the EMT-inducing transcription factor ZEB1; under genotoxic stress, ZEB1 facilitates USP7-mediated CHK1 stabilization, enhancing homologous recombination repair and conferring radioresistance. Overall, USP7 serves as a regulatory node that connects stemness self-renewal, EMT, and stress tolerance across different tumor backgrounds through substrate-specific mechanisms.

In addition to serving as a potential CSC marker in various cancers, ubiquitin-specific protease 22 (USP22) plays a critical role in coordinating transcriptional networks, driving Myc-induced transformation, and regulating cell-cycle progression. It also promotes the maintenance of CSC properties by sustaining Hes1 expression (32). Its depletion induces G1-phase arrest, highlighting its significant role in proliferation. In pancreatic cancer, USP22 drives EMT by upregulating N-cadherin, VIM, ZEB1, and Snail, while simultaneously suppressing E-cadherin (33). Mechanistically, USP22 deubiquitinates and stabilizes SIRT1, which subsequently inhibits STAT3 acetylation and modulates downstream targets such as MMP9 and Twist. In colon cancer cells, USP22 silencing similarly disrupts this SIRT1/Twist/MMP9 axis (34), thereby reinforcing its role in coupling stemness, EMT, and invasive behavior.

Overall, aberrant DUB activity not only enhances CSC properties but also strengthens functional crosstalk between CSCs and EMT by stabilizing EMT regulators. Consequently, selectively targeting specific DUBs has emerged as a potential therapeutic strategy aimed at dissociating these phenotypes and inhibiting tumor metastasis and relapse. Notably, functional redundancy among DUBs is a critical confounding factor in both mechanistic exploration and translational research. For instance, in the β-catenin signaling cascade, multiple DUBs have been reported to stabilize the same pathway effector molecules across diverse tumor backgrounds. This convergence suggests that the phenotypic impact of inhibiting a single DUB may vary significantly depending on tumor type, CSC status, and underlying signaling network architecture. In certain scenarios, a specific DUB may serve as the dominant enzyme for β-catenin deubiquitination due to differential expression levels, subcellular localization, or preferential recruitment of specific scaffold proteins; in such instances, single-agent inhibition alone may be sufficient to disrupt EMT and stemness. Conversely, in other contexts, parallel DUB activities may buffer pathway output, where blockade of one enzyme is partially compensated by others, resulting in limited therapeutic efficacy. Therefore, the effectiveness of DUB-targeted therapies depends not merely on whether a given DUB can deubiquitinate β-catenin, but more critically on whether that DUB acts as a non-redundant signaling node within a specific cellular milieu. To circumvent CSC plasticity, future DUB-targeted therapies should integrate biomarker-driven stratification strategies to precisely identify rate-limiting DUBs, combined with combinatorial approaches to overcome overlapping compensatory networks.

Distribution of EMT-related DUB targets in different tumors
More than 90% of human cancers originate from epithelial cells, which form tightly packed cell layers through specialized junctional structures such as tight junctions and adherens junctions. In contrast, mesenchymal cells lack organized layering, exhibit loose contact with neighboring cells, and possess strong migratory capacity. EMT refers to the process by which epithelial cells transform into mesenchymal cells, representing a hallmark of tumor invasion and metastasis (35). Phenotypically, EMT is characterized by the dissolution of intercellular junctions and increased motility; molecularly, it is defined by the suppression of epithelial proteins like E-cadherin and the induction of mesenchymal markers such as VIM (36). DUBs are extensively involved in the EMT process across various tumor types. Table 1 summarizes the currently reported EMT-associated DUBs and their major targets in different cancers.

DUBs regulate key signaling pathways mediating EMT and stemness maintenance
DUBs support the maintenance of CSC stemness and EMT phenotypes by modulating the stability, subcellular localization, and biological activity of components in multiple developmental signaling pathways. Among these, Wnt/β-catenin, Hh, Notch, and TGF-β signaling pathways are particularly important because they cooperatively regulate cell fate determination, phenotypic plasticity, invasion, and therapy resistance. In this section, we summarize current evidence regarding DUB-mediated regulation of major EMT- and stemness-associated pathways (Figure 2).

DUBs and the Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway
The canonical Wnt signaling pathway is a crucial regulator of EMT and tumor stem cell phenotypes. It regulates downstream gene expression through both the β-catenin-dependent canonical pathway and noncanonical signaling pathways (37). Aberrant activation of Wnt signaling is frequently observed during tumor progression (38), and the protein stability of β-catenin is dynamically regulated by the balance between E3 ubiquitin ligases and DUBs, thereby influencing Wnt signaling activity. Multiple E3 ubiquitin ligases are involved in modulating the stability of core Wnt pathway components, including β-catenin, APC, and DVL. Correspondingly, multiple DUBs functionally modulate these proteins through deubiquitination. For example, USP14 removes K63-linked polyubiquitin chains from DVL, reducing its ubiquitination level and activating Wnt/β-catenin signaling (39). Conversely, CYLD functions as a negative regulator of Wnt signaling, and its loss promotes β-catenin recruitment and pathway activation (40). Other DUBs exert regulatory effects at distinct nodes of this pathway. USP4 participates in Wnt signaling regulation by targeting NLK and TCF7L2, while USP34 has been reported to negatively regulate Wnt activity by maintaining the stability of AXIN1/2 and protecting these components of the degradation complex from ubiquitin-dependent degradation (41). TRABID is another Wnt-associated deubiquitinating enzyme that can deubiquitinate APC and modulate the stability of the β-catenin/TCF transcriptional complex (42). These findings indicate that DUB-mediated regulation extends beyond β-catenin itself, affecting multiple structural and regulatory layers of this pathway.

In fact, several DUBs, including USP9X, USP47 and USP4, have been reported to directly deubiquitinate β-catenin (43–45). DUB-mediated receptor regulation also affects cellular responses to Wnt signaling. USP8 (also known as UBPY) promotes the recycling of Frizzled (Fzd) to the plasma membrane by deubiquitinating Fzd, thereby maintaining receptor availability (46). Similarly, USP6 can deubiquitinate Fzd and low-density lipoprotein receptor-related protein 6 (LRP6), and inhibit the activity of the transmembrane E3 ubiquitin ligases RNF43/ZNRF3, thereby increasing the abundance of Fzd and LRP6 on the plasma membrane and enhancing cellular sensitivity to Wnt signals (47).

At the transcriptional level, DUBs can indirectly potentiate Wnt signaling by stabilizing β-catenin co-activators. For instance, USP5 promotes the accumulation of Forkhead box M1 (FoxM1) by removing ubiquitin chains from FoxM1 and preventing its degradation. Stable FoxM1 further facilitates the recruitment of β-catenin to Wnt target gene promoters, thereby enhancing transcriptional activation (48). In the absence of Wnt ligands, β-catenin is phosphorylated by the GSK3/AXIN/APC degradation complex, subsequently ubiquitinated by E3 ligases such as RNF220, and degraded by the proteasome. When Wnt ligand is present, this complex dissociates to protect β-catenin from degradation; meanwhile, USP7 interacts with RNF220 to promote β-catenin deubiquitination and enhance its stability, thereby further amplifying Wnt signal transduction (49). Importantly, β-catenin stabilized by DUBs not only drives EMT but also transcriptionally activates glycolytic enzymes such as PKM2, thereby coupling structural plasticity with metabolic adaptation. Crucially, the stabilizing effect of specific DUBs on β-catenin extends far beyond canonical EMT induction. Following nuclear translocation, stable β-catenin functions as a pivotal transcriptional co-activator, upregulating critical glycolytic transporters and enzymes such as GLUT1, PKM2, and LDHA (50). Therefore, by rescuing β-catenin from proteasomal degradation, DUBs essentially couple EMT-driven morphological changes with the high metabolic demands (e.g., aerobic glycolysis) required for cancer stem cell maintenance. Consequently, DUB-mediated stabilization of β-catenin not only promotes EMT but also enforces glycolytic reprogramming, linking developmental signaling to metabolic adaptation in CSCs.

DUBs and the Hh signaling pathway
The Hh pathway is another developmental signaling cascade closely associated with CSC stemness and EMT. Key components of the Hh pathway, including Patched (PTCH), Smoothened (SMO), and glioma-associated oncogene homolog (Gli) family proteins, are all subject to precise regulation by ubiquitination. SMO is a signal transducer of the Hh pathway localized at the plasma membrane: activated SMO transduces signals into the cytoplasm to initiate downstream signaling cascades, while polyubiquitination of SMO inhibits this signal transduction process, and DUB-catalyzed deubiquitination promotes SMO protein accumulation and subsequent Hh pathway activation. RNA interference (RNAi) screens in Drosophila and mammalian cell culture models revealed that USP8 directly deubiquitinates SMO, thereby driving SMO accumulation and downstream Hh signal activation. Notably, in the absence of Hh ligand, USP8 stabilizes SMO without altering its phosphorylation status, and SMO accumulation induced by USP8 remains under inhibitory regulation by PTCH. These findings suggest that USP8 exerts regulatory effects downstream of SMO phosphorylation events, yet remains constrained by upstream regulatory mechanisms of the Hh pathway (51).

Nuclear effector functions of the Hh signaling pathway are primarily mediated by the transcription factor Cubitus interruptus (Ci) in Drosophila and Gli family proteins in mammals. In Drosophila, Ci is regulated by two distinct ubiquitination-dependent pathways: in the absence of Hh ligand, Ci undergoes partial degradation mediated by the Slimb-Cullin1/β-transducin repeat-containing protein (β-TrCP) complex; upon Hh stimulation, Ci degradation mediated by the Hib-Cullin3-Roadkill complex finely tunes its transcriptional activity (52). In mammalian cells, Gli family proteins are similarly regulated by ubiquitination modifications, including ubiquitin binding catalyzed by the E3 ubiquitin ligase Itch (53).

USP7 competitively binds to Ci/Gli with its endogenous negative regulators Cos2 and Suppressor of Fused (Sufu), while Hh signaling promotes phosphorylation of Ci/Gli by enhancing the binding affinity between USP7 and Ci/Gli. By antagonizing Ci/Gli ubiquitination mediated by the Slimb-Cullin1/β-TrCP family E3 ubiquitin ligases, USP7 stabilizes Ci/Gli proteins and facilitates Hh signal transduction. Consistent with this regulatory mechanism, knockdown of USP7 in a cerebellar medulloblastoma model significantly inhibited the sonic hedgehog (SHH) pathway activity and reduced Gli protein expression levels (54).

USP21 has been identified as a positive regulator of Hh signaling. Genetic knockout of USP21 in mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) significantly attenuated Hh pathway activation induced by SMO agonists. In human embryonic kidney 293 T (HEK293 T) cells transfected with GLI1, USP21 depletion reduced GLI1 promoter-driven reporter gene activity and modulated PKA-dependent Gli1 phosphorylation, collectively indicating that USP21 regulates Gli function through multiple distinct mechanisms. In addition to USP family DUBs, CYLD is also closely associated with tumorigenesis related to the Hh pathway. Downregulation of CYLD expression is frequently observed in basal cell carcinoma (BCC), a phenotype driven in part by the hyperactivation of Gli1/2. Mechanistically, aberrantly activated Gli1 transcriptionally upregulates the expression of the zinc-finger transcription factor Snail, which in turn transcriptionally represses CYLD, ultimately forming an oncogenic positive feedback loop (55). Taken together, DUBs exert multi-target and multi-layered regulation on the Hh pathway by modulating the stability and activity of the two signaling nodes, SMO and Ci/Gli. Importantly, the hyperactivation of the Hh/Gli axis maintained by these DUBs not only drives EMT but also triggers profound metabolic reprogramming. For instance, stable Gli1 can directly upregulate key metabolic enzymes such as hexokinase 2 (HK2) (56), suggesting that DUB-mediated amplification of Hh signaling equips CSCs with enhanced glycolytic capacity necessary for survival in nutrient-deprived tumor microenvironments. However, in pathological contexts such as BCC, the regulatory roles of other DUBs on PTCH and the entire Hh signaling cascade remain to be further elucidated. Therefore, Hh activation driven by DUBs combines EMT induction with enhanced glycolytic capacity, supporting the survival of CSCs in metabolically hostile niches.

DUBs and the Notch signaling pathway
The Notch signaling pathway is a highly conserved intercellular communication pathway that is widely active during embryonic development and in a range of adult tissues. It maintains tissue homeostasis by regulating cell differentiation, proliferation, and apoptosis, and also participates in the EMT process. The local microenvironment can influence Notch activity, and dysregulation of this pathway is closely associated with various diseases, including developmental disorders and cancers (57). Beyond its involvement in cellular plasticity, emerging evidence suggests that aberrant activation of Notch signaling may influence CSC metabolism, including c-Myc-dependent glutaminolysis and glycolysis, potentially supporting increased bioenergetic requirements. Consequently, DUBs that modulate the stability of the Notch intracellular domain (NICD) may function as context-dependent regulators linking Notch-associated EMT phenotypes to metabolic adaptation in CSCs.

Canonical Notch activation is initiated by the binding of membrane-bound ligands on donor cells to Notch receptors on adjacent recipient cells, which triggers sequential proteolytic cleavage and releases the NICD. NICD subsequently translocates to the nucleus, where it forms a transcriptional activation complex and induces the expression of downstream target genes. These signaling events are primarily mediated by DSL family ligands, including Delta, Serrate/Jagged, and LAG-2, although several non-canonical ligands have also been reported; their mechanisms of action are not fully understood (57). Among the DUBs implicated in this pathway, USP12 has emerged as a negative regulator of Notch signaling. Studies show that silencing USP12 impairs Notch lysosomal trafficking, leading to the accumulation of Notch receptors on the cell surface and enhanced pathway activation. Further biochemical evidence indicates that USP12 forms a complex with its cofactor UAF1 to negatively modulate Notch signaling by deubiquitinating the inactive form of the receptor (58). CYLD also participates in the regulation of Notch signaling and its downstream effects on EMT. In T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL) cell lines, it has been reported that the Notch-Hes1-CYLD axis can activate the IKK complex, thereby potentiating NF-κB signaling (59). In addition, CYLD can negatively regulate the expression of the ligand JAG2 through interaction with the E3 ubiquitin ligase MIB2. Loss of CYLD increases JAG2 levels and enhances Notch activity, subsequently promoting the upregulation of Snail and N-cadherin, thereby facilitating the acquisition of EMT-associated phenotypes (29, 60). Collectively, the Notch signaling pathway is tightly controlled by ligand-receptor interactions and ubiquitination modifications, and plays a context-dependent bidirectional role in tumorigenesis and EMT progression. Therefore, a deep understanding of how DUBs such as USP12 and CYLD modulate Notch signaling can not only provide mechanistic insights into their role in malignant progression but also lead to the discovery of new therapeutic targets and intervention strategies for cancer treatment.

Regulation of the TGF-β signaling pathway by DUBs and their role in EMT
As a ubiquitous cytokine, TGF-β regulates key processes such as cell growth, differentiation, and survival across multiple lineages, notably being recognized as a factor of the EMT program (61). Initiation of TGF-β signaling fundamentally relies on specific interactions between its ligand and trimeric high-affinity membrane receptors, namely TβRI, TβRII, and TβRIII (β-glycan). Upon receptor activation, TβRII and TβRI cooperate to induce phosphorylation of Smad2 and Smad3. Phosphorylated Smad2/3 proteins subsequently form complexes with Smad4 and translocate to the nucleus to drive transcription of target genes (61). In addition to the canonical Smad-dependent pathway, TβRI can also activate non-canonical signaling cascades, including Ras-related signaling mediated by adaptor proteins such as ShcA, Sos1, and Grb2 (62). Notably, the TGF-β signaling pathway, composed of components such as TβRI, TβRII, and Smads, is strictly regulated by the UPS (63). As a key component of this system, DUBs regulate TGF-β signaling activity and the EMT process by removing ubiquitination modifications from pathway components. USP4 is a structurally and functionally conserved DUB that modulates TGF-β signaling and EMT progression via multiple molecular mechanisms. On the one hand, USP4 directly deubiquitinates TβRI while inhibiting the ubiquitination and degradation of Smad7, and it can also maintain its own protein stability through self-deubiquitination (64). In a zebrafish xenograft model, USP4 enhances TGF-β signaling to promote invasion and metastasis of breast cancer cells, whereas USP4 knockdown significantly attenuates TGF-β-induced EMT in breast cancer cells. On the other hand, in colorectal cancer, USP4 interacts with PRL-3, which is a key stimulator of the EMT signaling pathway. Through deubiquitination, USP4 stabilizes PRL-3 expression and activates the Akt signaling pathway, ultimately leading to the downregulation of E-cadherin. High expression of PRL-3 has been confirmed to be closely associated with poor prognosis in cancer patients (65).

USP11 is another positive regulator of TGF-β signaling. It modulates TGF-β signaling by targeting the interaction between Smad7 and TβRI. Consistent with this mechanism, USP11 binds to Smad7 and masks its negative regulatory function while enhancing pathway activity through deubiquitination of TβRI. Knockdown of USP11 reduces TGF-β-induced Smad2/3 phosphorylation levels, thereby inhibiting the EMT process in mouse MECs (66). Similarly, using a multifunctional RNAi screening approach, Eichhorn et al. further identified USP15 as a key regulator of the TGF-β signaling pathway. USP15 interacts with the Smad3-Smurf3 complex and stabilizes TβRI through deubiquitination, thereby enhancing TGF-β signal transduction (67).

OTUB1 also modulates TGF-β signaling, albeit through a slightly different mechanism. It interacts with E2 ubiquitin-conjugating enzymes, blocking the transfer of ubiquitin from E2 to E3 ligases, thereby inhibiting the ubiquitination-mediated degradation of phosphorylated Smad2/3. In colorectal cancer cells SW480, Western blot analysis showed that OTUB1 knockdown increased the expression of ZEB1, β-catenin, N-cadherin, and VIM, while decreasing the level of E-cadherin, indicating that OTUB1 plays an important role in TGF-β-mediated gene transcription and cell migration (68). Furthermore, AMSH-2, a DUB containing an AMSH domain, is widely expressed in cells. Overexpression of AMSH-2 may activate the TGF-β promoter, and co-immunoprecipitation experiments have demonstrated interactions between AMSH-2 and both Smad7 and Smad2, suggesting a potential regulatory role in the TGF-β signaling pathway (69). Available evidence further suggests that prolonged DUB-associated TGF-β/SMAD signaling may influence not only the EMT program but also aspects of metabolic rewiring. For instance, activated SMAD complexes have been reported to affect mitochondrial dynamics and promote the Warburg effect, meeting the energy demands of migrating CSCs (70, 71). Collectively, these observations raise the possibility that DUBs associated with the TGF-β axis may contribute to the coordination of cellular plasticity and metabolic adaptation, although the underlying mechanisms and their relevance across tumor contexts require further investigation.

Crosstalk between DUBs and transcription factors: a bidirectional network regulating EMT and stemness
DUBs and transcription factors may form a multilayered, bidirectional regulatory network involved in the EMT process, CSC-associated properties, chemoresistance, and metastatic potential. Extensive evidence suggests that EMT and its associated transcription factors are central drivers of tumor cells acquiring CSC-like properties (72). For example, the key EMT transcription factor Twist1 can simultaneously mediate EMT in breast cancer, maintain CSC self-renewal, promote tumor metastasis, and reduce the sensitivity of cancer cells to chemotherapeutic agents (73). Notably, Twist1 is also a key driver of tumor metabolic reprogramming, particularly in promoting the Warburg effect. Thus, DUB-mediated stabilization of these transcription factors may provide one mechanism through which phenotypic plasticity and metabolic adaptation are coordinately regulated. By modulating the ubiquitination and stability of EMT-associated and stemness-related transcription factors, DUBs may function as context-dependent regulatory nodes connecting EMT, tumor stemness, and therapeutic resistance.

Among DUBs that positively regulate transcription factor stability, members of the USP family are particularly prominent. USP29 stabilizes the Twist1 protein through deubiquitination, thereby promoting the progression of triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) (73). USP4 simultaneously stabilizes β-catenin and Twist1 in colorectal cancer cells, enhancing tumor stemness and inducing chemoresistance (74). UCHL3 maintains the tumorigenic potential and stemness features of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) by enhancing the stability of β-catenin (75). USP21 specifically removes K48-linked ubiquitin chains from the stemness transcription factor Nanog, preventing its proteasomal degradation and stabilizing the Nanog protein. This mechanism not only helps maintain embryonic stem cell pluripotency but also contributes to the regulation of pancreatic cancer stemness (76). In addition, USP22 is frequently overexpressed in lung cancer and other malignancies and is widely regarded as a marker associated with tumor stem cells; in gastric cancer, USP22 also maintains and enhances tumor stemness by stabilizing BMI1 (77).

In colon cancer tissues, OTUB2 expression is significantly elevated. OTUB2 knockdown attenuates stemness characteristics, increases sensitivity to oxaliplatin, inhibits EMT, and ultimately reduces metastatic potential. Mechanistically, OTUB2 specifically deubiquitinates the transcription factor SP1, inhibiting its K48-linked ubiquitination-mediated degradation and thereby maintaining its stability. SP1 subsequently binds to the 1,822–1,830 region of the GINS1 promoter and enhances its transcriptional activity. The resulting OTUB2-SP1-GINS1 axis plays a key role in driving colon cancer stemness, chemoresistance, and EMT (78). USP14 interacts directly with the stemness transcription factor SOX2 through its ubiquitin carboxyl-terminal hydrolase domain. USP14 knockdown increases polyubiquitination of SOX2 and reduces its stability, thereby impairing the maintenance of CSC markers (79). USP7 interacts with the basal transcription factor BTF3 and upregulates its protein level, thereby enhancing the EMT phenotype and stem cell-like characteristics of HCC cells (80). Moreover, USP28 regulates the stability of the transcription factor c-Myc, thereby inhibiting the growth of c-Myc-overexpressing neuroblastoma (NB) (81). Given that c-Myc is a key regulator of aerobic glycolysis and glutamine metabolism, DUB-mediated stabilization of c-Myc directly links the maintenance of rapid CSC proliferation with its required metabolic flexibility.

Notably, the interaction between DUBs and transcription factors is not limited to unidirectional control; they frequently participate in bidirectional feedback loops that finely tune CSC properties. For instance, in glioma stem cells, the key transcription factor E2F1 directly transactivates the expression of USP5. Conversely, USP5 maintains the post-translational stability of the stemness factor OCT4, thereby determining the self-renewal and tumorigenic capacity of these cells (82). Similarly, in ovarian cancer, c-Jun binds to the enhancer region of OTUD1 to promote its transcription. Elevated OTUD1 subsequently forms aggresomes, recruits the ASK1 kinase, and hyperactivates the JNK/c-Jun signaling cascade. This c-Jun-OTUD1 positive feedback loop is critical for maintaining the self-renewal and tumorigenicity of ovarian cancer stem cells (OCSCs) (83). Furthermore, the transcription factor AP-2 can directly drive the transcription of USP22. Clinically, a positive correlation between AP-2 and USP22 has been observed in lung cancer tissues, indicating that this regulatory axis is a fundamental driver of lung adenocarcinoma progression (84).

The EMT-TFs stabilized by these interconnected DUB networks may contribute not only to cellular dedifferentiation but also to metabolic reprogramming. For instance, DUB-stabilized SNAI1 and Twist1 have been shown to directly inhibit mitochondrial OXPHOS genes while cooperatively transactivating key glycolytic enzymes (85–87). Consequently, DUBs situated within these transcriptional circuits serve as molecular hubs. By simultaneously conferring mesenchymal traits, amplifying stemness, and rewiring metabolic fluxes, they could contribute to CSC plasticity and facilitate adaptation to stressful tumor microenvironments, potentially reducing sensitivity to conventional therapies.

The orchestration of metabolic rewiring by DUBs in CSCs
Rather than merely occurring as a passive consequence of EMT, metabolic alterations may also be subject to regulation by DUBs, including through changes in the stability of metabolic enzymes, transporters, and other metabolic regulators. By removing ubiquitin chains from specific metabolic proteins, DUBs may influence the metabolism of glucose, lipids, and amino acids, potentially contributing to the bioenergetic and biosynthetic requirements associated with phenotypic plasticity in CSCs. In addition, available evidence suggests that these metabolic programs may interact with stemness- and EMT-related signaling networks, potentially establishing reciprocal regulatory relationships associated with tumor progression and treatment resistance.

Reprogramming of glucose metabolism: the Warburg effect
Aerobic glycolysis, also known as the Warburg effect, is one of the most prominent metabolic features of CSCs. Although OXPHOS remains important in certain tumor contexts, many CSC populations preferentially rely on glycolysis to rapidly generate ATP and metabolic intermediates while limiting the accumulation of ROS (88). This metabolic phenotype is not only a result of oncogenic signaling but is also actively maintained by DUBs that stabilize rate-limiting glycolytic enzymes and glucose transport machinery (89).

Among the best-characterized mechanisms, multiple DUBs have been shown to regulate the abundance and activity of glycolytic enzymes such as phosphofructokinase (PFK), pyruvate kinase M2 (PKM2), and lactate dehydrogenase A (LDHA). PKM2 is frequently overexpressed in cancer and serves as a core regulator of the Warburg effect. In various types of cancer, multiple DUBs modulate the activity and stability of PKM2 by modulating its ubiquitination status. In colorectal cancer, OTUB2 inhibits the ubiquitination of PKM2 and enhances its enzymatic activity (89). In ovarian cancer, PSMD14 interacts directly with PKM2, reducing its ubiquitination level to maintain protein stability (90). In addition, USP20 (91) and USP7 (92) can also bind to PKM2 and regulate its ubiquitination homeostasis. In gastric cancer, USP4 interacts with PKM2 and catalyzes its deubiquitination; high expression of USP4 significantly promotes the proliferation, glucose uptake, and lactate production of gastric cancer cells (93). These findings suggest that DUBs do not merely act on isolated metabolic enzymes but integrate metabolic flux with stemness-associated transcriptional programs.

Emerging evidence supports the concept that DUBs can directly stabilize metabolic enzymes. In non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), OTUB2 promotes malignant progression and metabolic reprogramming through dual regulation. On the one hand, OTUB2 enhances proliferation, colony formation, migration, and invasion, thereby augmenting the malignant phenotype. On the other hand, it activates the Warburg effect and the AKT/mTOR signaling pathway, a classic pro-tumorigenic pathway that centrally regulates cellular growth and metabolic homeostasis. Mechanistically, OTUB2 directly binds to U2AF2 and removes its ubiquitin modifications, thereby stabilizing U2AF2 and preventing its proteasomal degradation. This regulatory mechanism is critical for OTUB2-driven NSCLC progression (94). Since CSCs are typically located in hypoxic and nutrient-deprived niches, the ability of DUBs to maintain the stability of glycolytic enzymes may provide a selective survival advantage by sustaining ATP production and the generation of biosynthetic precursors. Moreover, lactate accumulation resulting from enhanced glycolysis can acidify the tumor microenvironment, thereby promoting invasion, immune evasion, and EMT. Therefore, DUB-driven glycolytic rewiring serves as a metabolic axis maintaining CSC plasticity.

DUBs and amino acid metabolism in CSCs
Amino acid metabolism, particularly glutamine metabolic reprogramming, is a key mechanism by which CSCs adapt to metabolic demands and sustain unlimited proliferation. Glutamine not only serves as a primary carbon and nitrogen source for nucleotide synthesis, glutathione production, and the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle but also synergizes with enhanced antioxidant defense mechanisms to help cells resist oxidative stress and therapeutic damage. As important regulators of the UPS, DUBs, including USP13, USP9X, USP15, USP29, and USP39, can finely tune the synthesis, catabolism, and transport of glutamine by stabilizing relevant transcription factors, metabolic enzymes, and transporters. This reshapes the metabolic flux of α-ketoglutarate (α-KG), nucleotides, and lipids, promoting tumor cell survival, proliferation, and the maintenance of CSC stemness.

DUBs play crucial roles in regulating glutamine synthesis, catabolism, and transport across various cancers. In ovarian cancer, USP13 acts as a central driver of glutamine metabolic reprogramming by deubiquitinating and upregulating ATP citrate lyase and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase (α-KGDH), thereby coupling glutamine catabolism with mitochondrial respiration and fatty acid synthesis to supply energy and biosynthetic precursors to cells (95). Similarly, in NB, USP29 links glutamine catabolism to nucleotide synthesis, supporting cell proliferation; loss of USP29 disrupts the metabolism of glycolytic and nucleotide biosynthesis intermediates (96). In GBM, glutamine synthesis depends on the coordinated regulation of USP9X and HDAC6, where USP9X removes K48-linked ubiquitin chains from glutamine synthetase (GS) to stabilize the protein, while HDAC6 enhances its enzymatic activity and stability through deacetylation. Together, they maintain glutamine production under conditions of glutamine deprivation (97). In multiple myeloma, USP15 antagonizes CRL4(CRBN) E3 ligase-mediated GS ubiquitination, preventing its degradation; notably, USP15 is highly expressed in immunomodulatory drug (IMiD)-resistant MM cells, and silencing USP15 restores sensitivity to lenalidomide, indicating its significant role in metabolic regulation and drug resistance (98).

DUBs also regulate glutamine transport. Glutamine enters cells through transporters such as ASCT2/SLC1A5, is subsequently converted to glutamate by mitochondrial glutaminase, and is further metabolized into α-KG, thereby supplying rapidly proliferating cancer cells with ATP, biosynthetic precursors, and reducing equivalents (99). In NSCLC, the USP39-MRPL35-SLC7A5 axis represents a key pathway controlling glutamine uptake: USP39 stabilizes MRPL35 through deubiquitination, which in turn upregulates the glutamine transporter SLC7A5. Increased SLC7A5 expression significantly enhances glutamine uptake and metabolism, supporting NSCLC proliferation and invasion (100). Beyond glutamine metabolism, amino acid-dependent redox regulation is also closely associated with CSC survival and therapeutic resistance. However, direct evidence regarding the role of DUBs in regulating serine/glycine-derived one-carbon metabolism in CSCs remains limited. Current evidence more strongly supports the role of DUBs in amino acid-associated redox control, particularly through the regulation of the cystine/glutamate antiporter SLC7A11 and ferroptosis sensitivity. For example, BAP1 suppresses SLC7A11 expression through H2A deubiquitination at the SLC7A11 promoter, thereby limiting cystine uptake and rendering cancer cells sensitive to ferroptosis (101). Conversely, OTUB1 stabilizes SLC7A11, promoting cystine uptake, glutathione biosynthesis, and ferroptosis resistance (102). These findings indicate that DUBs regulate amino acid-dependent redox homeostasis through specific mechanisms.
