Whether specific DUB-substrate pairs directly control serine/glycine pathway enzymes, such as phosphoserine aminotransferase 1, phosphoserine phosphatase, or methylenetetrahydrofolate dehydrogenase family, in CSCs remains an important area for future research.

DUBs and lipid metabolic rewiring in CSCs
Reprogramming of cholesterol metabolism is a key characteristic enabling cancer cells to meet biosynthetic demands and maintain CSC stemness. Aberrant activation of key pathways—such as the mevalonate pathway and pathways regulating cholesterol uptake and synthesis—is closely associated with tumor progression. Recent studies have confirmed that DUBs can reprogram cholesterol metabolic flux in cancer cells by stabilizing key regulators of cholesterol metabolism and modulating pathway activities, thereby influencing tumor proliferation, drug resistance, and the maintenance of CSC stemness. These findings provide new molecular mechanisms and potential targets for metabolism-based cancer therapies.

DUBs regulate cholesterol uptake and synthesis pathways. During lipid uptake, ubiquitin carboxyl-terminal hydrolase 1 (UCHL1) stabilizes the scavenger receptor CD36 through deubiquitination. CD36 not only mediates the uptake of oxidized low-density lipoprotein (oxLDL) to promote foam cell formation—a key event in atherosclerosis—but also regulates lipid uptake, including cholesteryl esters, in various cancers (103). Studies have shown that knockdown or inhibition of UCHL1 increases K48-linked ubiquitination of CD36 and promotes its proteasomal degradation, thereby reducing oxLDL uptake and foam cell formation (103). Although its direct role in cancer has not yet been fully established, CD36-mediated metabolic reprogramming is crucial for energy supply in tumor cells, suggesting that UCHL1 may regulate cholesterol-related lipid metabolism in tumor cells through CD36 and indirectly participate in EMT.

BAP1 is a component of the polycomb repressive deubiquitinase complex (PR-DUB) and is frequently lost in malignant mesothelioma and various other cancers. BAP1 can indirectly regulate cholesterol biosynthesis via PRC2, and its loss creates a therapeutic window known as “PRC2-dependent cholesterol metabolism vulnerability”. Meanwhile, BAP1 deficiency leads to significant upregulation of cholesterol biosynthesis-related proteins, including mevalonate pathway enzymes, in the liver, accompanied by hypercholesterolemia and hepatic lipid depletion (104). As BAP1 is a classic tumor suppressor gene, dysregulation of its control over cholesterol synthesis may establish a metabolic basis for hepatic tumorigenesis, indicating that BAP1-mediated cholesterol metabolic reprogramming could be a potential driver of early carcinogenesis (104).

USP28 is highly expressed in squamous carcinomas such as lung squamous cell carcinoma and shows a significant positive correlation with protein levels of SREBP2, a key transcription factor regulating cholesterol synthesis, and is associated with poor patient prognosis (105). Mechanistically, USP28 directly binds the mature form of SREBP2 and stabilizes it by removing its K48-linked ubiquitin chains, thereby activating the mevalonate pathway. This pathway not only synthesizes cholesterol but also produces isoprenylation substrates such as geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate, providing essential protein modification substrates for cancer cell proliferation and CSC stemness maintenance (105). Functional studies show that USP28 knockdown reduces mevalonate pathway flux and increases cancer cell sensitivity to statins, which are inhibitors of this pathway, while supplementation with geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate can reverse the tumor-suppressive effects of USP28 deficiency (105). Furthermore, combined treatment with dual USP28/25 inhibitors and statins significantly inhibits the survival of squamous cell carcinoma, confirming USP28's status as a critical therapeutic target in the cholesterol metabolism-cancer growth axis (105).

The combined modulation of DUB activity and lipid metabolism has been explored as a potential therapeutic approach. In TNBC, USP14 promotes tumor cell survival by stabilizing the anti-apoptotic protein Survivin. The cholesterol metabolism inhibitor lovastatin was shown to interfere with the interaction between USP14 and Survivin, enhances Survivin's ubiquitination-mediated degradation, and induces apoptosis in TNBC cells (106). Moreover, combined use of USP14 inhibitors such as IU1 and lovastatin synergistically inhibits colony formation in TNBC cells, demonstrating that drugs targeting cholesterol metabolism can enhance antitumor efficacy by interfering with DUB-substrate interactions (106). BRCC3 (BRCA1/BRCA2-containing complex subunit 3) is another member of the DUB family, which has been implicated in Tet2-deficient clonal hematopoiesis. It remodels the inflammatory microenvironment by regulating cholesterol metabolites, thereby promoting tumor-associated pathologies such as atherosclerosis and potential hematological malignancies. However, its detailed mechanisms and connections to EMT and CSC remain to be further elucidated.

DUBs regulate cancer stem cell survival through ferroptosis
Ferroptosis is an iron-dependent, lipid peroxidation-driven form of regulated cell death. Its dysregulation is profoundly implicated in cancer progression, CSC maintenance, and therapy resistance (107). By modulating the ubiquitination homeostasis of key regulators in oxidative and metabolic pathways, DUBs serve as critical nodes connecting ferroptosis evasion and CSC stemness. Recent studies suggest that DUBs may contribute to the association between metabolic adaptation and ferroptosis resistance, although their specific relevance to CSC survival remains to be established. For instance, in TNBC, the USP24-DHODH axis has been implicated in the regulation of ferroptosis sensitivity (108). Mechanistically, USP24 stabilizes dihydroorotate dehydrogenase (DHODH), a mitochondrial enzyme critical for maintaining redox balance and detoxifying lipid peroxides. By retaining DHODH, USP24 provides a direct mechanism for CSC tolerance to severe treatments and oxidative stress. Beyond direct redox regulation, DUB-driven metabolic rewiring collaborates closely with epigenetic and post-translational networks to enhance stress tolerance. In gastric cancer, the PSMD14-PFKFB2-H3K27 lactylation cascade demonstrates how PSMD14-stabilized PFKFB2 enhances glycolytic flux (109). Accumulated lactate reshapes the tumor metabolic microenvironment and drives H3K27 lactylation to activate stemness-associated transcription. Strikingly, this lactate-rich microenvironment can further trigger feed-forward loops to enhance ferroptosis resistance. A recent study on intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (ICC) revealed that L-lactate directly promotes K100 lactylation of PSMD14, shielding the DUB from proteasome-mediated degradation (110). Stable PSMD14 subsequently interacts with the glycolytic enzyme ENO1, removing its K63-linked ubiquitin chains and preventing its lysosomal degradation. This L-lactate/PSMD14/ENO1 positive feedback loop not only promotes sustained lactate production but also drives profound ferroptosis resistance, ultimately compromising the efficacy of anti-PD-1 immunotherapy. Thus, DUBs may link ferroptosis resistance with metabolic, epigenetic, and immune remodeling, potentially contributing to CSC plasticity.

Basic insights into ferroptosis regulation in stem cells also derive from normal physiological models, which typically share vulnerabilities with CSCs. For example, the histone deubiquitinase MYSM1 is critical for protecting normal hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) from ferroptosis (111). MYSM1 deficiency severely impairs protein synthesis, rendering HSCs highly susceptible to lipid peroxidation attacks, ultimately leading to bone marrow failure. Remarkably, in MYSM1-deficient models, pharmacological blockade of ferroptosis can completely rescue the HSC population and their function even without correcting the underlying protein synthesis defect (111). Because protein synthesis has been linked to ferroptosis sensitivity in human stem cells, elevated MYSM1 activity observed in some malignancies may also reduce ferroptosis sensitivity in CSCs, although this possibility remains to be tested. These findings suggest a potential association between histone deubiquitination and stem-cell survival under ferroptotic stress.

In solid tumor contexts, specific DUBs actively dismantle ferroptosis cascades to preserve CSC characteristics, providing viable therapeutic targets. In HCC, UCHL3 orchestrates ferroptosis evasion through the UCHL3-β-catenin axis (75). Elevated UCHL3 removes K48-linked polyubiquitin chains from the ARM domain of β-catenin, preventing its proteasomal degradation. This stabilization not only drives HCC proliferation and stemness but also actively suppresses ferroptosis by attenuating the accumulation of ROS and malondialdehyde (MDA). Consequently, targeting UCHL3 with TCID promotes β-catenin degradation, strongly triggers ferroptosis, and restricts tumor growth, underscoring this axis as a key vulnerability in HCC (75).

Similarly, targeting DUBs can simultaneously activate multiple cell death pathways to overcome CSC resistance. In ovarian cancer, elevated USP2 is associated with poor prognosis, and its pharmacological blockade reveals a multi-layered regulation of tumor cell death. The small-molecule inhibitor ML364 of USP2 simultaneously triggers apoptosis (via downregulation of cyclin D1 and PARP cleavage) and ferroptosis (via a sharp increase in intracellular ROS levels) (112). The antitumor efficacy of ML364 depends on the ferroptosis pathway, confirming the role of USP2 as a dual-modulator of apoptosis and ferroptosis. Collectively, these studies indicate that targeting DUB-associated regulation of ferroptosis may warrant further investigation as a potential approach for reducing CSC survival (Figure 3).

Bidirectional interactions between epigenetic regulation and metabolites
Cancer stem cell plasticity is regulated not only by transcription factors and developmental signaling pathways but also by the dynamic interplay between cellular metabolism and the epigenetic machinery. Metabolic pathways generate substrates and cofactors required for chromatin-modifying enzymes, thereby enabling nutrient availability, oxygen tension, mitochondrial function, and redox status to influence DNA methylation and histone modifications (113). Conversely, epigenetic regulators alter the expression of metabolic enzymes and transporters, generating reciprocal feedback loops that stabilize stem-like, mesenchymal, and therapy-resistant cellular states (114). DUBs reside at the nexus of this network, as they regulate both the stability or activity of epigenetic regulators and the stability or activity of metabolic signaling proteins (115).

Histone modifications and DNA methylation
Beyond transcriptome remodeling, epigenetic dysregulation—including DNA methylation and histone post-translational modifications (HPTMs)—has been extensively demonstrated to be closely associated with cancer initiation and progression (116). Under physiological conditions, these epigenetic mechanisms precisely regulate DNA packaging and chromatin formation, thereby maintaining genomic stability. In cancer, however, the dysregulation of these processes disrupts this balance and drives malignant transformation. Notably, the reversibility of epigenetic regulation makes it a focal point in current efforts to overcome cancer drug resistance (116). Within the context of CSC biology, epigenetic regulation is particularly important because it provides a reversible mechanism that enables cancer cells to dynamically transition between stem-like and differentiated states, adapt to microenvironmental pressures, and acquire therapy-tolerant phenotypes. Thus, DUB-mediated DNA methylation and histone modifications should be viewed not merely as general features of tumor progression but as critical regulatory layers maintaining CSC and phenotypic plasticity. Importantly, these epigenetic processes are tightly coupled to cellular metabolism, as many chromatin-modifying enzymes require metabolites as substrates or cofactors (117). Therefore, metabolic rewiring can directly influence chromatin accessibility and transcriptional plasticity during EMT-associated CSC maintenance. In some cancers, the expression of the tumor suppressor CYLD is suppressed by epigenetic mechanisms, including DNA methylation and histone deacetylase (HDAC)-mediated histone deacetylation. For example, in gastric adenocarcinoma, hypermethylation of the CYLD promoter region significantly downregulates the expression of CYLD mRNA and protein, thereby eliminating its tumor-suppressive function (118).

DNMT1 is a core epigenetic regulator responsible for maintaining DNA methylation homeostasis and plays a critical role in preserving parental DNA methylation patterns after replication. USP7 serves as an epigenetic modulator of DNMT1-dependent DNA methylation, exhibiting dual functions in both maintenance and de novo DNA methylation; in vitro assays demonstrate that USP7 can enhance the methyltransferase activity of DNMT1 by approximately two-fold (119). Meanwhile, evidence suggests that this epigenetic regulation is closely linked to EMT-metabolic crosstalk. Specifically, USP7-stabilized DNMT1 can silence the promoters of epithelial genes, such as CDH1 which encodes E-cadherin, thereby promoting the EMT process. Simultaneously, DNMT1-mediated hypermethylation has been shown to repress metabolic genes, including FBP1, which encodes fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase 1, promoting a metabolic shift toward aerobic glycolysis (120). Through this coordinated epigenetic mechanism, the USP7-DNMT1 axis acts as a node that links mesenchymal traits with the metabolic rewiring supporting CSC migration and survival.

In hepatoblastoma (HB), USP7 forms a novel ternary protein complex with UHRF1 and DNMT1 (121). This complex specifically binds to the promoters of key tumor suppressor genes in HB—including HHIP (Hedgehog-interacting protein), IGFBP3 (insulin-like growth factor binding protein 3), and SFRP1 (secreted frizzled-related protein 1)—and transcriptionally represses these genes through the cooperative regulation of DNA methylation (promoter hypermethylation) and histone modifications (such as H3K27 deacetylation), thereby promoting the malignant progression of HB (121). In addition, USP10 also plays an important regulatory role in NSCLC. The protein stability of HDAC7 is directly maintained by USP10-mediated deubiquitination, which protects it from degradation. Once stabilized, HDAC7 orchestrates the nuclear accumulation of β-catenin, enabling it to interact with TCF4 to drive transcriptional activation. The β-catenin–TCF4 complex activates the transcription of fibroblast growth factor 18 (FGF18), ultimately promoting NSCLC proliferation, invasion, and metastasis through FGF18-mediated signaling pathways (122). Inhibition of USP10 significantly accelerates HDAC7 degradation and impairs the growth and migratory capacity of NSCLC (122). These findings further indicate that DUB-mediated epigenetic regulation is functionally linked to signaling pathways in CSC biology, including the Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway and the transcriptional repression of tumor-suppressive programs. More broadly, by stabilizing epigenetic modifiers or remodeling chromatin-associated complexes, DUBs may promote stemness maintenance, EMT-associated plasticity, and adaptation to therapeutic stress, rather than merely supporting bulk tumor growth.

Histone ubiquitination and chromatin plasticity
Histone ubiquitination is a key component of epigenetic regulation, and its dynamic balance is maintained jointly by ubiquitin ligases and DUBs. DUBs regulate gene expression associated with CSC stemness by specifically removing ubiquitin chains from histones such as H2A, H2B, H3, and H4. Ultimately, this process affects biological characteristics such as self-renewal, differentiation potential, drug resistance, and metastatic ability. Importantly, chromatin plasticity is a central determinant of CSC adaptability, because it enables rapid and reversible reprogramming of lineage identity, stress responses, and invasive behavior. From this perspective, histone-directed DUB activity is not only an epigenetic housekeeping process but also a mechanism that may directly influence whether tumor cells retain stem-like features or transition into therapy-persistent and metastasis-competent states. In addition, USP38 regulates the deacetylase activity of HDAC1 through deubiquitination, participating in the DDR, particularly non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) repair, and playing a critical role in maintaining genomic integrity and cancer cell resistance to genotoxic stress (123). Given the close association between efficient DNA damage repair and the survival of CSCs following chemotherapy or radiotherapy, this chromatin-centered DUB function may also contribute to the persistence of therapy-resistant CSC populations under therapeutic pressure.

Metabolite-dependent epigenetic regulation and metabolic-epigenetic feedback
Cellular metabolism directly shapes the epigenetic state by controlling the availability of substrates and cofactors required by chromatin-modifying enzymes. Acetyl-CoA supplies acetyl groups for histone acetyltransferases (124), while S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) serves as a methyl donor for DNA and histone methyltransferases (125). Conversely, α-KG is an essential cofactor for ten-eleven translocation (TET) DNA demethylases and Jumonji C-domain histone demethylases (126, 127). The oncometabolite 2-hydroxyglutarate (2-HG), along with accumulated succinate and fumarate, can competitively inhibit α-KG-dependent dioxygenases, thereby promoting DNA and histone hypermethylation (126, 128). In parallel, the NAD+/NADH balance influences NAD⁺-dependent sirtuin deacetylases (129). These represent the precise biochemical mechanisms by which metabolic reprogramming alters chromatin accessibility, transcriptional plasticity, and the maintenance of EMT-associated CSC states.

This relationship is bidirectional rather than linear. Epigenetic regulators control the transcription of glucose transporters, mitochondrial enzymes, lipid-metabolic enzymes, and amino acid-metabolic pathways, while the resulting metabolic changes modify intracellular levels of acetyl-CoA, SAM, α-KG, NAD+, and oncometabolites, feeding back to act on chromatin-modifying enzymes (114). DUBs may connect these processes by regulating the stability or activity of epigenetic and metabolic effectors. For example, the USP28-LSD1 and USP22-SIRT1 axes discussed above illustrate how DUB-dependent stabilization of chromatin regulators maintains stemness and EMT-associated transcriptional programs (19, 34). Similarly, DUB-mediated stabilization of β-catenin, c-Myc, HIF-1α-related signaling components, or metabolic enzymes may reshape glycolysis, glutaminolysis, and mitochondrial metabolism, indirectly changing the metabolite pool available for epigenetic reactions (115). Therefore, DUBs should be viewed as context-dependent modulatorsof metabolic-epigenetic feedback rather than isolated regulators of histone ubiquitination.

However, it is necessary to distinguish these indirect regulatory links from direct metabolite-dependent control of DUB catalytic activity. Compared to the established roles of acetyl-CoA, SAM, α-KG, 2-HG, succinate, fumarate, and NAD + in specific chromatin-modifying reactions, there is currently insufficient evidence that these metabolites directly bind to DUBs or regulate their catalytic domains under physiological conditions. Changes in DUB abundance or activity following metabolic perturbation may result from alterations in transcription, localization, post-translational modifications, redox status, or substrate availability. Thus, demonstrating direct metabolite-DUB regulation requires pure enzyme kinetic studies, direct-binding assays, structural studies, and cellular rescue experiments using catalytic or metabolite-binding-deficient mutants. Until such evidence is obtained, direct metabolic control of DUB activity should be regarded as a plausible but unproven mechanism in CSC plasticity.

Therapeutic potential of targeting DUBs
DUBs have emerged as highly attractive therapeutic targets in oncology due to their critical roles in stabilizing stemness-associated oncogenic transcription factors, metabolic regulators, and signaling components. Unlike conventional cytotoxic agents that primarily eliminate rapidly proliferating bulk tumor cells, therapies targeting DUBs hold promise for disrupting molecular circuits maintaining CSC homeostasis, EMT, metabolic plasticity, and treatment resistance. Given that many DUBs occupy key nodes downstream of multiple signaling pathways, pharmacological inhibition of these enzymes could simultaneously suppress tumor stemness, diminish metastatic capacity, and re-sensitize resistant tumors to conventional therapies. Importantly, DUBs are also enzymatically druggable. Numerous members of the USP, UCH, OTU, and JAMM families possess catalytic domains or ubiquitin-binding pockets suitable for small-molecule targeting. Over the past decade, several DUB inhibitors have entered preclinical development, with a few advancing to early clinical evaluation. Although no anti-cancer drugs specifically targeting DUBs have been approved for clinical use yet, accumulating evidence strongly supports the translational potential of this therapeutic strategy, particularly in combination regimens aimed at overcoming chemoresistance, radioresistance, and adaptive metabolic reprogramming. Beyond conventional catalytic inhibitors, an emerging and conceptually distinct strategy involves the development of deubiquitinase-targeting chimeras (DUBTACs), a class of molecules that extends the therapeutic scope from DUB inhibition to DUB-mediated selective protein stabilization. Unlike small molecules that globally inhibit DUB activity or block substrate binding, DUBTACs are heterobifunctional molecules designed to recruit selected DUBs to target proteins, thereby promoting deubiquitination of the target and protecting it from proteasomal degradation. This modality is particularly compelling in cancer and stemness research, as it enables the restoration of proteins with tumor-suppressive, pro-differentiation, or sensitization functions, which are typically unstable in aggressive tumors. Recent studies have established proof-of-concept DUBTAC platforms based on OTUB1, USP7, and USP28, highlighting the feasibility of selectively repurposing DUBs as a therapeutic strategy. Rather than simply shutting down DUB activity, DUBTACs offer the possibility of substrate-directed reprogramming of ubiquitin-dependent signaling pathways. In microenvironments where indiscriminate DUB inhibition is limited by toxicity or pathway redundancy, this approach could potentially improve target selectivity and expand the therapeutic window, although these benefits require further preclinical and clinical validation.

Among existing compounds, inhibitors targeting proteasome-associated DUBs and USP family members have attracted the most attention. b-AP15 is one of the earliest reported small-molecule inhibitors targeting the proteasome-associated DUBs USP14 and UCHL5/UCH37. By blocking deubiquitination at the 19S regulatory particle of the proteasome, b-AP15 induces the accumulation of polyubiquitinated proteins, proteotoxic stress, endoplasmic reticulum stress, and oxidative damage, ultimately triggering apoptotic cell death (130). In models of multiple myeloma and various solid tumors, b-AP15 has demonstrated significant antitumor activity, including efficacy against bortezomib-resistant cells, suggesting that DUB inhibition may overcome resistance mechanisms associated with classical proteasome inhibitors (131). VLX1570 is a clinical-stage derivative of b-AP15 that similarly targets USP14 and UCHL5, showing potent anti-myeloma activity in preclinical studies (132). This agent has entered early-phase clinical trials in patients with relapsed/refractory multiple myeloma (133), representing one of the earliest attempts to translate DUB inhibition into cancer therapy. However, its clinical development was halted due to dose-limiting toxicities. These toxicities primarily stem from its Michael acceptor-mediated off-target covalent binding and the narrow therapeutic window associated with pan-inhibition. To overcome these bottlenecks, drug development has shifted toward highly selective, non-covalent allosteric inhibitors.

Another extensively investigated compound is the selective USP7 inhibitor P5091. USP7 stabilizes multiple oncogenic substrates, including MDM2, β-catenin, EZH2, c-Myc-associated regulatory factors, and stemness-related transcriptional networks, thereby promoting CSC survival, facilitating EMT, participating in DNA damage repair, and mediating tumor drug resistance (134–137). Preclinical studies have demonstrated that P5091 induces apoptosis and inhibits tumor growth in hematological malignancies, including multiple myeloma, chronic lymphocytic leukemia, and lymphoma (138–140). Moreover, USP7 inhibition has been shown to attenuate stem-like phenotypes, impair homologous recombination repair, and sensitize tumor cells to DNA-damaging agents, providing a potential strategy for reversing chemotherapy and radiotherapy resistance. In parallel, next-generation USP7 inhibitors and related derivatives, such as FT671, FT827, GNE-6640, and GNE-6776, have further advanced the concept of selective targeting of DUBs (141). Other DUB inhibitors have also demonstrated therapeutic potential in experimental models. For example, mitoxantrone has been reported to inhibit USP11, thereby interfering with DNA damage repair signaling and sensitizing tumor cells to poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP) inhibitors (142). Compounds such as ML323 can inhibit USP1 and destabilize substrates involved in DNA repair and stemness maintenance, representing a potentially effective strategy to enhance the efficacy of platinum agents, PARP inhibitors, and radiotherapy (143). Similarly, inhibitors targeting USP10, USP13, and UCHL1 are currently in active preclinical research stages.

Therapeutic targeting of DUBs is closely linked to EMT, CSC biology, and metabolic plasticity. Beyond directly inducing tumor cell death, DUB-targeted strategies may effectively disrupt plastic cell states that drive metastasis and disease relapse. Numerous DUBs stabilize transcription factors that induce EMT and their upstream signaling pathways. For instance, USP22, USP29, USP4, and USP7 have all been implicated in maintaining EMT-like and stem-like phenotypes across various tumor types. Pharmacological inhibition of these DUBs can suppress tumor cell migration and invasion, reduce tumorsphere formation, and impair tumor-initiating capacity. MitoCur-1 is a curcumin derivative initially designed to selectively target tumor mitochondria and induce redox imbalance; it has recently been identified as a novel USP14 inhibitor. It exerts antitumor activity by inducing ferroptosis in melanoma cells and significantly sensitizes vemurafenib-resistant cells (144). Given the significant phenotypic plasticity of CSCs, DUB inhibition alone is typically insufficient to eradicate tumors. Therefore, these findings underscore the necessity of developing rational combination therapies to enhance anti-tumor efficacy. First, dual-targeting strategies can be employed within the DDR network. For instance, specific DUBs such as USP1 are critical for double-strand break repair. Combining USP1 inhibitors (such as KSQ-4279) with PARP inhibitors or platinum-based chemotherapy can induce synthetic lethality, effectively reversing chemoresistance in BRCA-proficient tumors. Second, therapeutic regimens can be designed to co-target the DUB-metabolism-ferroptosis axis. Since CSCs heavily rely on metabolic reprogramming and ferroptosis evasion to cope with therapeutic stress, combining DUB inhibitors with metabolic antagonists represents a highly promising strategy. For example, the recently discovered mechanism by which the USP24-DHODH axis drives ferroptosis resistance in TNBC provides a theoretical basis for combining selective USP24 inhibitors with ferroptosis inducers, a method that can metabolically deplete CSCs and dismantle their plasticity (Figure 4).

Conclusion and future prospects
The considerable plasticity of CSCs remains an important challenge to achieving durable therapeutic responses. In this context, DUBs may serve as regulatory nodes involved in CSC homeostasis. Rather than functioning solely as regulators of protein stability, DUBs may also modulate the context-dependent interplay between EMT and metabolic reprogramming. By stabilizing selected components of developmental signaling pathways (such as Wnt/β-catenin, Hh, Notch, and TGF-β) and chromatin modifiers, DUBs may connect the phenotypic changes associated with invasion to metabolic adaptations that support survival under stressful tumor microenvironmental conditions. Changes in DUB localization, activity, or substrate recognition in response to microenvironmental stress may therefore contribute to CSC plasticity and therapeutic resistance.

Central hypothesis and key open questions
Importantly, DUB-substrate interactions are not simple “one DUB, one substrate” relationships but are highly context-dependent, shaped by subcellular localization, scaffold proteins, and cellular metabolic states. This regulatory complexity creates several challenges for therapeutic translation. Broad-spectrum DUB inhibition may cause systemic toxicity, while structural homology within catalytic domains hinders the development of highly selective small-molecule inhibitors. Consequently, we propose that precise targeting of the DUB-EMT-metabolism axis—potentially using emerging approaches such as deubiquitinase-targeting chimeras (DUBTACs) or rational combination strategies—may provide a means of limiting CSC-associated plasticity. By shifting from global enzyme blockade to substrate-directed ubiquitin editing, DUBTACs can selectively restore proteins that antagonize EMT, inhibit stemness, or sensitize tumors to therapeutic stress. However, whether these approaches can sufficiently restrict CSC metabolic and phenotypic plasticity while avoiding off-target effects and functional redundancy remains to be established.

To overcome the remaining translational barriers, future research should complement descriptive substrate catalogs with mechanistic studies of DUB selectivity. Several key questions remain to be addressed: Regarding dynamic substrate specificity, it is essential to determine how individual DUBs alter their substrate preferences (e.g., between EMT-transcription factors and metabolic enzymes) in response to distinct microenvironmental cues (such as hypoxia and acidic pH) or therapeutic stress.For spatiotemporal mapping, future studies should determine whether integrating spatial transcriptomics with single-cell metabolic profiling can define the precise spatiotemporal trajectories of DUB activity within heterogeneous CSC subpopulations during metastasis and acquired resistance.Concerning the translational optimization of DUBTACs, future studies should determine how to improve their tissue penetration, target selectivity, and bio-stability of these molecules to achieve potent in vivo efficacy against CSCs without triggering broad UPS toxicity.Regarding patient-specific model validation, future studies should determine whether integrating patient-derived organoids (PDOs) with single-cell multi-omics approaches can adequately model the spatiotemporal patterns of DUB activity within patient-specific tumor microenvironments.Ultimately, addressing these questions may support the identification of predictive biomarkers and more informative patient stratification, as well as the evaluation of rational combination strategies integrating targeted DUB modulation with conventional chemoradiotherapy, targeted agents, or immunotherapy.

paper.title: Molecular and Immune Features of Metastatic Prostate Cancer in Hispanic and Non-Hispanic American Men.
paper.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Prostate cancer (PCa) is the most common solid tumor in American men, with persistent ethnic disparities, particularly among Hispanic American (HA) men. The tumor microenvironment (TME) and tumor genomics may contribute to disease progression but remain undercharacterized in HA populations.

METHODS: We conducted a retrospective exploratory analysis of 83 patients with treatment-naïve metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer who underwent next-generation sequencing (NGS). Tumor genomic alterations, immune profiles, pathway activity, and clinical characteristics were compared between HA and non-Hispanic White (NHW) patients.

RESULTS: Compared with NHW patients, HA patients presented with higher PSA levels (111.5 vs. 52.6 ng/mL, p = 0.02), and more advanced disease, including T4 tumors (41% vs. 14%, p = 0.01) and visceral metastases (41% vs. 16%, p = 0.04). Pathway analyses identified increased KRAS (FDR = 0.02), Hedgehog (FDR = 0.04), and NOTCH (FDR = 0.07) signaling in HA tumors. HA tumors exhibited higher expression of stem cell markers (ALDH1A1, ALDH1A2, PROM1) and immunoinhibitory genes (PDCD1LG2, FOXP3) (all p < 0.05), along with increased infiltration of M1 macrophages (0.72% vs. 0%) and natural killer (NK) cells (4.84% vs. 3.55%, all p < 0.05 and q < 0.10). HA tumors demonstrated higher expression of genes associated with drug efflux (ABCC1, ABCB1), EMT (TWIST1, MMP2), cell cycle (CCND2), apoptosis inhibition (BIRC2, XIAP), and epigenetic regulation (EP300, TET1, TET2) (all p < 0.05 and q < 0.10). Clinically, HA patients initiated therapy earlier (1 vs. 3 months, p ≤ 0.01), had a longer interval to second-line therapy (20 vs. 11 months, p < 0.05), and had shorter follow-up (23 vs. 44 months, p = 0.03).

CONCLUSIONS: HA patients demonstrated differences in genomic alterations, pathway activity, and tumor immune features compared with NHW patients. Given the study's modest sample size and observational design, these findings should be considered hypothesis-generating and warrant validation in larger prospective cohorts with broader representation of Hispanic American men.
paper.full_text:
Introduction
Prostate cancer (PCa) is the most common solid organ malignancy and the second leading cause of cancer‐related mortality among men in the United States [1, 2]. Racial and ethnic disparities in PCa outcomes are well documented. Black/African American men experience a disproportionately high burden of disease, with higher incidence and mortality rates than other racial groups, and have consequently been the focus of many studies investigating biological and socioeconomic contributors to PCa disparities [3]. Hispanic‐American (HA) men also experience disparities in presentation and outcomes compared with non‐Hispanic White (NHW) men, and remain substantially underrepresented in genomic and tumor microenvironment studies [4, 5, 6, 7].

While earlier studies emphasized social determinants of health as primary contributors to PCa disparities, accumulating evidence suggests that biological differences may also be associated with disease presentation and progression across racial and ethnic groups [8, 9]. Emerging evidence further suggests that epigenetic alterations, including differences in DNA methylation, chromatin remodeling, and gene expression regulation, may contribute to prostate cancer disparities by influencing tumor aggressiveness and treatment response across populations [10]. Advances in genomic profiling have identified molecular heterogeneity in prostate tumors that may correlate with differences in clinical behavior. However, most large‐scale genomic studies have predominantly included men of European ancestry, limiting the understanding of tumor biology in underrepresented populations, including HA men [11].

Emerging evidence from multiple cancer types suggests that racial and ethnic groups may exhibit distinct molecular tumor characteristics. Studies of hepatocellular, colorectal, gastric, lung, pancreatic, and central nervous system tumors have identified differences in genomic alterations, oncogenic pathway activation, and potentially actionable biomarkers among Hispanic patients and other underrepresented populations [12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17]. Collectively, these findings highlight the importance of characterizing the molecular landscape of historically underrepresented populations to improve understanding of cancer biology and advance precision oncology.

The tumor microenvironment (TME), comprising stromal cells, immune cells, and vasculature, plays a critical role in tumor development, progression, and metastasis [18]. PCa is a biologically heterogeneous disease. Prostatic epithelial cells serve as the primary site of tumor development; however, prostate cancer progression is influenced not only by malignant epithelial cells but also by their interactions with surrounding stromal cells, immune cells, blood vessels, and extracellular matrix components. Reciprocal signaling among these cellular populations can promote tumor growth, invasion, metastasis, immune evasion, and therapeutic resistance, highlighting the importance of the tumor microenvironment in prostate cancer pathogenesis and progression [19]. Alterations in cytokine signaling, immune infiltration, and stromal remodeling have been shown to influence tumor growth and therapeutic response [20].

Recent studies have demonstrated that TME features differ across racial and ethnic groups and may influence PCa progression [19, 21]. Differences in immune response, stress response, cytokine signaling, and chemotaxis pathways have been observed in the TME of African American (AA) and NHW men, affecting fibroblast remodeling and angiogenesis [9, 21, 22, 23, 24]. These observations suggest that tumor‐associated stromal and immune responses differ across populations and may be associated with variation in disease presentation and outcomes. Although molecular and immune differences have been increasingly characterized in African American and non‐Hispanic White populations [1, 8, 9, 22, 24], comparable data in Hispanic American men remain limited. Consequently, the genomic, transcriptomic, and tumor microenvironment features of metastatic prostate cancer in this population remain poorly defined.

In this retrospective study, the primary objective was to characterize genomic, transcriptomic, and tumor microenvironment features of metastatic hormone‐sensitive prostate cancer in Hispanic American men compared with non‐Hispanic White men. Secondary exploratory objectives included evaluating differences in oncogenic signaling pathways, immune cell composition, and clinical characteristics between groups.

Patient Cohort and Clinical Data Collection
We conducted a retrospective analysis of 83 patients diagnosed with synchronous or metachronous metastatic treatment‐naive hormone‐sensitive prostate adenocarcinoma (mHSPC) who underwent next‐generation sequencing (NGS) of primary prostate gland tissue using the MI Profile‐MI Cancer Seek (Caris Life Sciences) and presented to the University of Arizona Cancer Center (UACC) between 2015 and 2023. For the purposes of this study, treatment‐naive refers to the absence of prior androgen deprivation therapy or other systemic hormonal therapy exposure at the time of tumor sampling. Primary tumor specimens were obtained before exposure to hormone‐directed therapy and were used for molecular profiling. Prior local therapies, including prostatectomy, radiation therapy, or neoadjuvant treatment, were permitted.

As the institution's Institutional Review Board (IRB) had provided a waiver of informed consent, informed consent was not obtained from patients included in this study. The IRB approval number was STUDY00000053. Patients were eligible for inclusion if they had histologically confirmed prostate adenocarcinoma, synchronous or metachronous metastatic or locally advanced hormone‐sensitive disease, available comprehensive Caris next‐generation sequencing (NGS) results, clinical documentation through at least first‐line hormone‐sensitive therapy, and documented self‐reported race and ethnicity in the medical record. Patients were excluded if they had a non‐predominant prostate cancer histology (including small cell, large cell neuroendocrine, squamous cell, adenoid cystic, stromal sarcoma, or other rare subtypes), localized disease managed with curative intent or active surveillance, unavailable or incomplete NGS data, insufficient clinical documentation to assess study outcomes, or missing race and ethnicity information.

Clinical and demographic data were abstracted from the electronic medical records in a de‐identified manner. Variables collected included age at presentation, race, ethnicity, obesity (defined as a body mass index ≥ 30 kg/m2), personal and family cancer history, Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status, smoking status, alcohol use, and illicit drug use. Pathologic features at diagnosis included prostate‐specific antigen (PSA) level, Gleason grade, and tumor stage according to the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) 8th edition TNM classification. Treatment‐related variables included surgery, radiation, standard‐of‐care systemic treatment, and participation in clinical trials.

Clinical outcome data were collected to characterize treatment patterns and response kinetics. These included time from diagnosis to initiation of first‐line therapy, type of first‐line therapy administered, and time to PSA response following treatment initiation. Subsequent treatment patterns were recorded by assessing the interval from initiation of first‐line therapy to the initiation of second‐line treatment. Median overall survival was not reached at the time of analysis due to limited event occurrence and ongoing follow‐up for the majority of patients.

Next Generation Sequencing (NGS)
NGS was performed on genomic DNA isolated from formalin‐fixed paraffin‐embedded (FFPE) prostate cancer samples by a commercial CAP/CLIA lab using the NextSeq or NovaSeq 6000 platforms (Illumina Inc., San Diego, CA). For NextSeq sequenced tumors, a custom‐designed SureSelect XT assay was used to enrich 592 whole‐gene targets (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA). For NovaSeq sequenced tumors, a panel of more than 700 clinically relevant genes was sequenced at high coverage and high read‐depth, along with another panel designed to enrich for additional > 20 000 genes at a lower depth. All variants were detected with > 99% confidence based on allele frequency and amplicon coverage, with an average sequencing depth of coverage of > 500× and an analytic sensitivity of 5%. Prior to molecular testing, tumor enrichment was achieved by harvesting targeted tissue using manual microdissection techniques.

Genetic variants identified were interpreted by board‐certified molecular geneticists and categorized as “pathogenic,” “likely pathogenic,” “variant of unknown significance,” “likely benign,” or “benign” according to the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ACMG) standards. Mutation assessment of individual genes stratified mutations as “pathogenic” and “likely pathogenic.” TMB was measured by counting all mutations found per tumor that had not been previously denoted as germline alterations in dbSNP151, Genome Aggregation Database (gnomAD) databases, or benign variants identified by Caris geneticists. A cutoff level of > 10 mutations per MB was used to characterize tumors as TMB high.

Fusion Detection
Fusions were analyzed using the ArcherDx FusionPlex Panel (ArcherDx, Boulder, CO), a target‐enrichment sequencing assay that utilizes Anchored Multiplex PCR with unidirectional gene‐specific primers to simultaneously detect and identify known and novel gene fusions. Libraries were created for use in NGS using ArcherDx reagents. After library preparation and indexing, samples were pooled and sequenced in a single reaction on the Illumina MiSeq system (Illumina, San Diego, CA). Sequencing data was de‐multiplexed and linked with the respective specimen by index for downstream fusion analysis using ArcherDx Analysis Software. All sequences were aligned to the human reference genome hg19. In order to qualify as “detected,” gene fusions were required to have ≥ 2 unique start sites and be in‐frame. Samples with < 20 000 unique RNA reads were reported as indeterminate and excluded from analysis. Off‐target hits and irrelevant novel isoforms were also excluded.

Whole Transcriptome Sequencing (WTS)
FFPE specimens underwent pathology review to diagnose percent tumor content and tumor size; a minimum of 10% of tumor content in the area for microdissection was required to enable enrichment and extraction of tumor‐specific RNA. A Qiagen RNA FFPE tissue extraction kit (Germantown, MD) was used for extraction, and the RNA quality and quantity were determined using the Agilent TapeStation (Santa Clara, CA). Biotinylated RNA baits were hybridized to the synthesized and purified cDNA targets, and the bait‐target complexes were amplified in a post capture PCR reaction. The resultant libraries were quantified, normalized, and the pooled libraries were denatured, diluted, and sequenced; the reference genome used was GRCh37/hg19 and analytical validation of this test demonstrated ≥ 97% Positive Percent Agreement (PPA), ≥ 99% Negative Percent Agreement (NPA), and ≥ 99% Overall Percent Agreement (OPA) with a validated comparator method. For transcript counting, transcripts per million (TPM) numbers were generated using the Salmon expression pipeline. RNA‐deconvolution was performed via quanTIseq to assess immune cell infiltration within the tumor microenvironment (TME) [25].

Epigenetic regulators evaluated included histone modifiers (EZH2, EP300, BRD2, BRD3, BRD4, HDAC1, SIRT1, and KDM1A) and DNA modifiers (DNMT1, DNMT3A, TET1, TET2, and TET3). Stem cell‐associated markers include ALDH1A2, PROM1, CD44, ALDH1A3, ALDH1A1, SOX2, NANOG, KLF4, and POU5F1.

T cell inflamed scores were calculated using T cell inflamed gene expression signature consisting of 160 genes, as previously described [26]. Interferon‐gamma (IFN‐γ) scores were calculated with a validated 18‐gene panel (CL5, CD27, CD274 (PD‐L1), CD276 (B7‐H3), CD8A, CMKLR1, CXCL9, CXCR6, HLA‐DQA1, HLA‐DRB1, HLA‐E, IDO1, LAG3, NKG7, PDCD1LG2 (PDL2), PSMB10, STAT1, and TIGIT) [27]. Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) was conducted to examine the enrichment or depletion of groups of genes associated with different biological pathways. This analysis was performed using Broad Institute software. GSEA was performed for biologically relevant pathways including KRAS, Hedgehog, NOTCH, WNT/β‐catenin, androgen response, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, epithelial‐to‐mesenchymal transition, apoptosis, hypoxia, angiogenesis, IL6/JAK/STAT3. IL2‐STAT5, p53, and TGF‐β signaling.

Immunohistochemistry
Immunohistochemistry of PD‐L1 (SP142 clone), MLH1 (M1 clone), MSH2 (G2191129 clone), MSH6 (44 clone), and PMS2 (EPR3947 clone) was completed on FFPE tissue slides. Slides were stained as per the manufacturer's instructions (Ventana Medical Systems Inc., Tucson, AZ) and were optimized and validated per CLIA/CAP and ISO requirements. Staining was scored for intensity (0 = no staining; 1+ = weak staining; 2+ = moderate staining; 3+ = strong staining) and staining percentage (0%–100%). The complete absence of protein expression of any of the 4 proteins tested (0+ in 100% of cells) was considered deficient MMR. A board‐certified pathologist independently evaluated all IHC results.

Statistical Analysis
Descriptive statistics were used to summarize clinical and molecular characteristics of the cohort. Continuous variables were compared using Student's t‐tests or Wilcoxon rank‐sum tests, as appropriate based on data distribution. Categorical variables were analyzed using chi‐square or Fisher's exact tests. Time‐to‐event outcomes were evaluated using the Kaplan–Meier method. Statistical significance was defined as a two‐sided p‐value < 0.05 and an FDR‐adjusted q‐value < 0.10. Given the exploratory nature of this study and the sample size, analyses were considered hypothesis‐generating.

Clinical and Demographic Characteristics of the Study Cohort
This study cohort included 83 patients with mHSPC, of whom 32 self‐identified as HA. There was no difference between HA and NHW patients in the age at presentation (median 66 years), race (90% white), marital status (64% married), obesity (40% with body mass index > 30 kg/m2), personal cancer history (10%), or first‐degree family history of cancer (48%). HA patients had a higher frequency of smoking (69% vs. 54%) and alcohol or drug use (63% vs. 45%) compared to NHW patients (p = 0.04).

At presentation, a higher proportion of HA patients had an ECOG performance status of 0 compared with NHW patients (56% vs. 22%, p = 0.001). HA patients also presented with higher PSA levels (median 111.5 vs. 52.6 ng/mL, p = 0.02) and more advanced disease, including higher rates of T4 tumors (41% vs. 14%, p = 0.01) and visceral metastases (41% vs. 16%, p = 0.04). There were no significant differences between HA and NHW patients in the frequency of a Gleason score > 4 (79% vs. 73%, p = 0.61) or nodal involvement (N1: 69% vs. 61%, p = 0.85). Most patients presented with synchronous metastatic disease, while only two patients had metachronous metastatic progression. Owing to the limited number of metachronous cases, subgroup analyses based on timing of metastatic presentation were not performed. Additional demographic, clinical, and pathologic characteristics stratified by ethnicity are presented in Supplemental Table 1.

Comparative Genomic Landscape of HA and NHW Tumors
Tumors from HA patients demonstrated a higher frequency of TMPRSS2‐fusion compared with tumors from NHW patients (46.4% vs. 20.0%, p = 0.04) (Figure 1). Differences in the frequency of other genomic alterations, including TP53, SPOP, and CTNNB1 mutations, were observed but did not reach statistical significance. NHW tumors showed lower absolute frequencies of loss of heterozygosity (LOH), CDK12 alterations, and RB1 alterations compared to HA tumors, though these differences were not statistically significant.

Tumor Immune Microenvironment Features
Immune deconvolution analysis demonstrated differences in immune cell composition between HA and NHW tumors. HA tumors showed higher infiltration of M1 Macrophages (0.72% vs. 0%, p < 0.05) and natural killer (NK) cells (4.84% vs. 3.55%, p < 0.05), along with lower infiltration of CD8 T cells (0% vs. 0.11%, p < 0.05) compared with NHW tumors (Figure 2). HA tumors also exhibited higher expression of the immunoinhibitory genes PDCD1LG2 (1.68‐fold, p < 0.05) and FOXP3 (1.45‐fold, p < 0.05). Moreover, there was no significant difference between HA and NHW in the T cell inflamed score (44 vs. −49, p = 0.14) and IFN‐y score (−0.5 vs. −0.45).

There were no significant differences between HA and NHW tumors in the frequency of PD‐L1 (10% vs. 2.1%, p = 0.29), mismatch repair deficiency or microsatellite instability high status (6.7% vs. 2.1%, p = 0.55), or high tumor mutational burden (4.0% vs. 4.5%, p = 1.0) (Supplemental Figure 1).

Pathway Enrichment Analysis
Gene set enrichment analysis demonstrated significant enrichment of Hedgehog signaling in HA tumors compared with NHW tumors (normalized enrichment score [NES]: 1.45, false discovery rate [FDR] = 0.04). Trends toward enrichment of NOTCH signaling (NES: 1.41, FDR = 0.07) and Wnt/β‐catenin signaling (NES: 1.38, FDR = 0.10) were also observed. Expression of pathway‐associated genes including WNT2, WNT1, HES1, and NOTCH1 was higher in HA tumors compared with NHW tumors (all p < 0.05 and q < 0.10) (Figure 3).

Stem Cell‐Associated Gene Expression
HA tumors demonstrated higher expression of stem cell‐associated markers including ALDH1A1 (2.1‐fold), ALDH1A2 (3‐fold), and PROM1 (1.6‐fold), compared with NHW tumors (all p < 0.05 and q < 0.10) (Figure 4).

Expression of Cancer Progression and Resistance Associated Genes
Compared with NHW tumors, HA tumors exhibited higher expression of genes associated with cell cycle regulation (CCND2), inhibition of apoptosis (BIRC2, XIAP), epithelial‐to‐mesenchymal transition (TWIST1, MMP2), and drug efflux (ABCC1, ABCB1), with fold changes ranging from 1.1 to 1.5 (all and q < 0.10) (Figure 5).

Treatment Patterns and Clinical Outcomes
Treatment modalities and sequencing did not differ significantly between HA and NHW patients (Supplemental Table 2). The median time from diagnosis to initiation of first‐line therapy was shorter among HA patients compared with NHW patients (1 vs. 3 months, p < 0.01) (Supplemental Figure 2A). Combination therapy was administered as first‐line treatment in 84% of all patients. Abiraterone plus androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) was used more frequently as first‐line therapy in HA patients compared with NHW patients (47% vs. 20%, p = 0.06), whereas ADT plus any AR blocker was more common in NHW patients (41% vs. 28%, p = 0.06).

Median PSA levels at three months following treatment initiation were lower in HA patients than in NHW patients (0.8 vs. 3.96 ng/mL, p = 0.05) (Supplemental Table 2). The median time to initiation of second‐line therapy was longer for HA patients compared with NHW patients (20 vs. 11 months, p = 0.05) (Supplemental Figure 2B). Median time to last clinical contact was shorter in HA patients than in NHW patients (23 vs. 44 months, p = 0.03) (Supplemental Figure 2C). Detailed treatment characteristics and outcomes by ethnicity are provided in Supplemental Table 2.

Discussion
In this retrospective clinicogenomic analysis of metastatic hormone‐sensitive prostate cancer, we identified differences in genomic alterations, pathway activity, and tumor immune features between HA and NHW cohorts. These findings provide a descriptive characterization of the molecular landscape in an underrepresented population and highlight several pathways and immune features that warrant further investigation. Our findings demonstrate that HA patients in this cohort presented with more advanced clinical disease and had differences in several molecular and immune features compared with NHW men. Specifically, HA patients had higher PSA levels, more advanced T and M stage disease, a higher frequency of TMPRSS2 gene fusions, increased expression of immunoinhibitory genes, and increased infiltration of M1 macrophages and NK cells. Additionally, HA tumors showed enrichment of oncogenic signaling pathways, stemness‐associated gene expression, and genes related to epithelial‐mesenchymal transition, cell cycle regulation, apoptosis resistance, drug efflux, and epigenetic modification. Together, these features reflect molecular patterns associated with aggressive tumor behavior in prior studies; however, the present analysis cannot establish their relationship to the more advanced clinical presentation observed in the HA cohort.

E26 Transformation‐Specific (ETS) gene family fusions were commonly observed in the HA cohort, including ERG, ETV1, and ETV4 rearrangements, with TMPRSS2 and SLC45A3 serving as fusion partners. The TMPRSS2‐ERG fusion is among the most frequent somatic alterations in prostate cancer, and it is thought to occur early in tumorigenesis [28]. Prior studies have demonstrated variability in the prevalence and mechanisms of ETS fusions across racial and ethnic groups, with the highest rates reported in men of European ancestry and lower rates in men of African and Asian ancestry [29]. However, the prevalence of ETS fusions in HA men has not been well described. Experimental data suggest that inflammatory signaling and oxidative stress may contribute to the formation of TMPRSS2–ERG rearrangements, raising the possibility that differences in inflammatory tumor environments may be associated with fusion frequency in specific populations [30]. The present study was not designed to evaluate the mechanisms underlying differences in fusion frequency. These observations should be considered hypothesis‐generating and require validation in independent cohorts.

Analysis of the tumor immune microenvironment revealed higher infiltration of M1 macrophages and natural killer (NK) cells, alongside lower CD8+ T‐cell infiltration, in HA tumors compared with NHW tumors. While M1 macrophages and NK cells are generally associated with anti‐tumor immune responses, persistent innate immune activation without effective adaptive immunity has been linked to tumor‐promoting inflammation and immune dysregulation in solid tumors [31, 32]. NK cells provide rapid cytotoxic responses, particularly against tumors with reduced major histocompatibility complex class I expression [33, 34]. However, tumors may adapt through immunosuppressive signaling, potentially limiting durable immune‐mediated control.

Consistent with the observed differences in immune cell composition, HA tumors demonstrated increased expression of immunoinhibitory markers, including PDCD1LG2 and FOXP3. A tumor microenvironment dominated by innate immune cells without sustained CD8+ T‐cell engagement may be associated with immune suppression over time [35]. These findings identify differences in immune composition and signaling between the study groups, although their relationship to tumor behavior and clinical outcomes remains uncertain. This study cannot determine whether these immune differences reflect ethnicity‐associated biology, differences in disease burden, or other clinical factors.

Pathway‐level analyses further demonstrated enrichment of Hedgehog signaling in HA tumors, with trends toward increased NOTCH and WNT/β‐catenin pathway activity. We observed upregulation of pathway‐associated genes, including WNT1, WNT2, HES1, and NOTCH1. These pathways have been implicated in prostate cancer stemness, EMT, and resistance to androgen receptor‐directed therapies in prior studies [36, 37, 38]. In addition, activation of WNT/β‐catenin signaling has been associated with T‐cell exclusion from the tumor microenvironment in prior studies [39, 40]. Although these previously described biological functions provide context for our observations, the present study cannot establish that pathway enrichment contributed to immune composition, treatment response, or clinical presentation. These findings instead identify candidate pathways for further investigation in HA prostate cancer.

HA tumors exhibited higher expression of cancer stem cell markers, including ALDH1A1, ALDH1A2, and PROM1, as well as genes associated with proliferation (CCND2), apoptosis resistance (BIRC2, XIAP), EMT (TWIST1, MMP2), and drug efflux (ABCC1, ABCB1). These molecular features have been associated with aggressive tumor behavior and therapeutic resistance in prior studies across cancer types.

Despite these molecular differences, HA and NHW patients received comparable systemic therapies. HA patients initiated first‐line therapy earlier and demonstrated more favorable initial PSA responses, yet had shorter follow‐up and evidence of more rapid progression. These findings suggest that while HA tumors may initially respond to androgen deprivation, underlying tumor biology may limit response durability.

HA patients had a longer interval to initiation of second‐line therapy than NHW patients, which may reflect sustained initial disease control or delayed recognition of progression. The retrospective design, selection bias related to NGS availability, incomplete clinical documentation, limited longitudinal outcome data, and shorter follow‐up among HA patients limit interpretation of these clinical outcomes. The modest sample size and potential confounders further constrain conclusions.

In addition, several baseline clinical characteristics differed between Hispanic American and non‐Hispanic White patients, including performance status, disease stage, visceral metastatic burden, smoking and substance use history, and duration of follow‐up. Given the modest sample size and exploratory nature of this study, multivariable analyses adjusting for these factors were not feasible. Furthermore, the limited sample size relative to the number of molecular and immune features evaluated would have increased the risk of model overfitting and unstable estimates. Consequently, the observed molecular and immune differences should be interpreted as unadjusted associations and may reflect, in part, differences in disease burden, clinical presentation, tissue selection, or other unmeasured factors rather than ethnicity alone. Accordingly, causal relationships between ethnicity, the observed molecular features, and clinical outcomes cannot be inferred. These findings should therefore be considered hypothesis‐generating and require validation in larger cohorts with sufficient power for multivariable analyses.

Strengths of this study include integrated genomic and immune profiling in a real‐world metastatic prostate cancer cohort and a focus on an underrepresented population. However, prospective studies with larger, ethnically diverse cohorts and longer follow‐up are needed to validate these findings. Overall, our results underscore the importance of incorporating Hispanic American men into clinicogenomic research and identify molecular and immune features that warrant further investigation in this population. These data support further investigation into biologically informed strategies to improve outcomes in high‐risk populations.

Conclusion
Our integrated molecular profiling of mHSPC identified differences in genomic alterations, pathway enrichment, and tumor immune features between Hispanic American and non‐Hispanic White patients. Hispanic American men demonstrated a higher prevalence of potentially actionable molecular features and a more advanced clinical presentation, findings that may be consistent with differences in tumor biology and disease characteristics. Given the retrospective design, modest sample size, and potential for residual confounding, these observations should be considered hypothesis‐generating. Validation in larger, multi‐institutional cohorts will be important to confirm these findings and to better understand the molecular features of prostate cancer in historically underrepresented populations.

paper.title: C2CD3 links tooth patterning to evolutionary tooth loss in birds and dental anomalies across vertebrates.
paper.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
paper.abstract: Primary cilia play an essential role in molecular signaling transduction during development, coordinating cell fate decisions and morphogenesis. Defects in components of the primary cilium result in an array of developmental syndromes called ciliopathies. Here we report 24 patients with nine rare and seven novel variants in the primary cilia gene C2CD3, which has previously been implicated in the ciliopathy Orofaciodigital syndrome XIV. Patients displayed an array of dental defects impacting the number, shape, and timing of tooth development. To understand the etiology underlying these defects, murine and avian models were analyzed during embryonic development. Ap2Cre;C2cd3ex4-5 fl/fl mouse mutants showed a range of dental defects prenatally, mimicking several of the phenotypes observed in patients. Shh was upregulated in the developing upper jaw, leading to a widening of the midline, while Shh expression in the lower jaw was reduced, highlighting the context-dependent impact of cilia on hedgehog signaling. In avian mutants carrying a C2CD3 variant, talpid2, tooth buds were evident with SHH expression upregulated during early development in both upper and lower jaws. Cartilage defects were additionally observed in both conditional mouse knockouts and talpid2 embryos. These changes in Shh signaling provide a mechanism to explain the phenotypes in patients and highlight the conserved role of C2CD3 in coordinating the morphogenetic potential of the jaw and patterning of the forming dentition. Given the conserved phenotypes, alterations in C2CD3-dependent ciliogenesis may have played a role in modulating Shh signaling to alter the timing and position of tooth germs across vertebrate evolution.

paper.title: Single-cell benchmarking separates epidermal stratification from appendage programme maintenance in an air-liquid interface skin model.
paper.abstract: Full-thickness skin equivalents (FTS) reproduce epidermal stratification, yet rarely generate hair follicles or glands. Defining the cellular features associated with this limitation could inform the engineering of appendage-bearing skin. Here we profiled mouse induced pluripotent stem cell-derived early epithelial progenitors (EEPs) and EEP-derived FTS by single-cell RNA sequencing, using developing mouse skin as a reference. FTS established a stratified epidermis with basal cell enrichment, but was accompanied by a marked reduction in appendage-primed cells (1.17% versus 8.69% in EEPs). Developmental mapping showed that FTS cells mapping to the hair follicle trajectory concentrated at early positions, whereas EEPs spanned a later and broader correspondence. Compared with matched developing skin states, FTS epithelium exhibited stronger injury-response and reactive transcriptional programmes. This epithelial reactivity coincided with an inferred dermal-epithelial signalling network with weaker BMP and noncanonical WNT inputs, no epithelial Hedgehog communication, and biased FGF and extracellular matrix interactions. Together, these findings link limited appendage formation in FTS to reduced appendage priming, a reactive interfollicular epidermal state, and a remodelled dermal signalling environment that diverges from native developmental niches.
